An estimation of the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay time for $B^0_s$ mesons has been made with the help of around 37 picobarns of LHCb data from 2010. This measure allows for constraints on theories beyond the Standard Model that may influence the $B^0_s$ system and was found to be 1.440 picoseconds by employing two methods with varying degrees of uncertainty, specifically 0.096 (statistical) ± 0.008 (systematic) ± 0.003 (model-based). Furthermore, a comparison with previous findings from D0 and CDF II revealed a more precise result, with a difference of around 0.5 standard deviations when considering the CDF II measurement, and an even greater discrepancy of 2.3 standard deviations for the D0 result. A sub-group of $B^0_s\rightarrow φφ$ decays was also identified and its decay time found to be 1.230 picoseconds with an uncertainty of 0.068 (statistical) ± 0.005 (systematic) ± 0.003 (model-based). A simulation of these processes in the Standard Model using the form factor $f_{+}(E)$ was also conducted and compared with the measured decay times, yielding a prediction of 1.286 picoseconds for $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decays and 1.260 picoseconds for $B^0_s\rightarrow φφ$ decays. A subsequent comparison with these predictions along with the measured decay times for $B^0_s\rightarrow μ^+μ^-$ and $B^0_s\rightarrow J/ψJ/ψ$ revealed that they lie within the limits set by the Standard Model, specifically above 10.63 TeV for the mass of the $B^0_s$ meson. The study involves a control problem formulated as the minimization of a cost function that includes the $L^2$ norm of the control variable, where the state equation is represented by the stochastic equation \begin{equation*} \begin{cases} dU_t=\left[ \sum_{k=1}^N S_k(U_t) \circ dW_t^k + f(U_t) \right] \circ dt + dW^0_t, \\ U_0=U_d, \end{cases} \end{equation*} where $\{W_t\}$ is a vector consisting of multiple stochastic processes, the functions $S_k$ vary depending on the state, and the initial condition is assumed to be stochastic. The paper demonstrates the existence of an optimal control for this problem and introduces a numerical discretization method based on a hybrid scheme that combines the finite element method for spatial discretization and the Euler scheme for temporal discretization, as well as a simulation using the Monte-Carlo method. The research also establishes the convergence of the hybrid scheme and provides a comparison with the Monte-Carlo method simulation. The paper addresses a significant shortcoming of the existing literature on stochastic control problems involving rough inputs and offers a novel approach to solving such problems. Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. At the higher end of our energy range, a specific anisotropy signal was initially reported - namely, a right ascension-based dipolar modulation. To further investigate, we divided the most energetic group into three segments, and discovered that this anisotropy becomes increasingly pronounced with rising energy levels above 4 EeV, exhibiting an energy-dependent pattern that adheres to a power law with an index of 0.79 ± 0.19. We also discovered that the orientation of these anisotropy patterns supports their extragalactic origins, across all energy levels examined. Furthermore, an investigation of quadrupolar components revealed that they lacked sufficient statistical significance. We interpret our findings within the context of theoretical models proposing the distribution of extremely energetic cosmic sources and cosmic magnetic field dynamics. And to that end, we propose that the sensitivity to polarization measurements capabilities at existing and future experiments, such as the Giant Auger Array and the Square Kilometre Array, may offer a means of directly observing these sources and better understanding the cosmic magnetic field's role in governing cosmic ray distribution. And finally, we note that the observed energy-dependent pattern may be attributed to a population of relativistic jets with particular energy thresholds. And in exploring alternative explanations, we investigated the anisotropy patterns that might be induced by large-scale structure, and found that while they could potentially account for the lowest energy group, they cannot explain the energy-dependent pattern observed across all energy levels examined. And in looking to the future, we propose that the study of extremely energetic cosmic ray distributions combined with quasars and galaxy cluster mappings, and the development of more sophisticated numerical simulations, will together provide a deeper understanding of cosmic magnetic field dynamics. And to that end, we are confident that the extensive datasets at existing and future experiments will offer vast opportunities for discovering new patterns of anisotropy in extremely energetic cosmic rays. And in doing so, we propose considering a range of energy groups at these experiments, from 4 EeV up to 100 EeV, in order to accurately capture the complex relationships between cosmic sources and cosmic magnetic field dynamics. And in exploring this further, we note that the sensitivity to composition measurements capabilities at these experiments, such as the Giant Auger Array and the Square Kilometre Array, may offer a means of combining distribution maps of extremely energetic cosmic sources with detailed numerical simulations of cosmic magnetic field dynamics

This study provides first-time data on the fluctuations of a specific angle, known as $\Psi_n$, and magnitude, known as $v_n$, related to particle flow, which have been determined using a newly developed technique for four-particle correlations. Researchers used ALICE to collect these data in high-energy Pb-Pb collisions at the LHC. Fluctuations in both angle and magnitude are evident across different centralities and become more pronounced in more central collisions and in collisions where the momentum of the particles is higher than 2 GeV/c. These findings, which have been compared to theoretical models such as iEBE-VISHNU, MUSIC, and AMPT, shed new light on the complex and not well understood initial conditions of these collisions. Furthermore, they highlight unique sensitivities to two crucial factors: the viscosity of quark--gluon plasma and the characteristics of the collisions' initial state. Given that these fluctuations tend to increase with the momentum of the particles, there is a need for re-examining existing theoretical models to gain a more precise and unbiased understanding of quark--gluon plasma's properties. Lastly, we have made these results available in the form of tables and figures that can be accessed separately.

This research focuses on addressing inconsistencies in data tables that contain missing values and functional relationships. Unlike conventional approaches that require adherence to these dependencies, our work aims to explore theories for handling instances that breach certain dependencies, with no preconditions on the presence of missing values. We establish a framework where each data entry can be associated with a truth status: true, false, inconsistent, or undetermined. Furthermore, our framework facilitates examination of pressing problems like data quality assessments, query validation, and data merging. Specifically, we investigate query validation as the central problem of this research, building on the foundation established by recent studies. Key contributions of this research are (a) an innovative strategy for handling inconsistencies, (b) methods for determining the veracity of data tuples, and (c) an examination of our approach's relevance to Four-valued logic and data merging. Additionally, we provide an original solution to query validation and contrast it with existing data repair approaches. Lastly, we offer a concise overview of our framework and its potential applications in database settings, along with two examples that demonstrate the practical utility of our framework. Moreover, we explore the connection between our approach and Four-valued logic, discuss issues of data merging, and examine our framework's capacity to handle nulls and functional dependencies in tables. Lastly, we conclude this research by identifying promising future work areas, including an examination of our approach's extension to recursive data tables, an investigation of Four-valued logic, and a discussion on the inclusion of integrity constraints within our framework. Our research indicates that a score-driven approach is particularly effective in capturing the evolution of time-varying parameters and allows for modeling complex dynamics and shifts within such data sets. Furthermore, we have analyzed the theoretical characteristics of the TV-PARX model, demonstrating under mild conditions that maximum likelihood estimation yields reliable and normally-distributed estimates of model parameters. To evaluate the TV-PARX model's performance and forecasting capabilities in real-world scenarios, we conducted a series of Monte Carlo simulations. Additionally, we have applied the time-varying specification of the TV-PARX model to empirical data sets, analyzing new daily COVID-19 cases in Italy and corporate defaults in the US. Our analysis of these data sets reveals valuable information on the time-varying dynamics of these datasets, and demonstrates the forensic capabilities of the TV-PARX model through the identification of key variables influencing these dynamics. The research findings presented herein contribute to the existing literature on dynamic econometric models, and the TV-PARX model framework can be applied to a variety of research and policy-related scenarios. We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that
replicates both object points and relative poses in relation to a target, using
category-level descriptors. We apply this representation in object manipulation,
with the aim of repeating tasks on new object instances from the same category
after witnessing a single demonstration. To achieve this, we use optimization
to locate the pose whose descriptor corresponds to that in the demonstration. NDFs
are efficiently trained without expert input, using a self-supervised 3D
auto-encoder, and exhibit robust performance across 6-DoF rotations and translations.
In experiments, NDFs master tasks from just a handful (5-10) demonstrations,
in both simulation and with a physical robot. Results show our method excels at
generalizing over different object instances and poses, surpassing a comparison
method relying on 2D descriptors. The NDF project is hosted at https://yilundu.github.io/ndf/.

These updated results confirm the functional renormalization group predictions made previously and support the idea that the universal exponent ratio marks the Yang-Lee edge in these universality classes. As such, this result has implications for searches of the Yang-Lee edge in lattice simulations of QCD. Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We initially employ a patch-based method to forecast projection heatmaps, representing the likelihood distribution of projected corners from 3D bounding boxes. Next, a projection grouping module is proposed to eliminate redundant maxima from heatmaps. Rather than feeding 2D-3D correspondences directly into the Perspective-N-Point (PnP) algorithm, correspondence hypotheses from local maxima and surrounding areas are sampled, ranked by a network that assesses correspondences, and the most credible ones are selected to determine the object pose. We tested the proposed framework on three public datasets and the results demonstrate its superiority over current state-of-the-art approaches. The proposed framework is termed DeepHMap++ and its code has been made publicly available. The proposed project grouping and correspondence learning concepts can also be applied to other object pose estimation tasks. The code has been made publicly available at: https://github.com/lingyu-0826/DeepHMap++_code. estimates a sparsely constructed inverse covariance matrix $\Theta$ from
multivariate Gaussian data $\mathcal{X}$, initially introduced by Dempster (1972)
under Covariance Selection. The framework has been expanded to accommodate
hidden variables in Chandrasekaran (2012) and can jointly estimate multiple
inverse covariance matrices, as shown in Danaher (2013) and Tomasi (2018). The

subcases like Graphical Lasso with latent variables, Group, and Fused Graphical Lasso. The package is available on GitHub, under the BSD-3 License. Numerous numerical methods for resolving stochastic differential equations in molecular dynamics simulations have been scrutinized and assessed, focusing on deterministic impulses, drifts, and Brownian motions. By utilizing the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff expansion, recent studies found that the methods' accuracy could be evaluated in terms of the impact of the step size on configurational averaging. Results showed that for harmonic oscillators, some methods yield precise configurational averages, potentially leading to better performance in biomolecular simulations, especially in cases where bond stretches play a crucial role. Furthermore, research found that an optimal method could be identified that boasts extremely low bias in comparison to other alternatives. Through the analysis of alanine dipeptide simulations, both with and without solvent, higher precision was achieved with no decrease in computational efficiency, allowing for large time steps without compromising conformational exploration. Ultimately, the most efficient method demonstrated enhanced molecular sampling, yielding overall improvements of at least 25% in feasible time steps in vacuum and reductions of at least a factor of ten in configurational average errors in solvent simulations with larger time steps. All in all, this research highlights a set of numerical methods that biologically relevant simulations can leverage to enhance accuracy while maintaining speed.

Our new method calculates a variation of eigenvector centrality for multi-layered networks that incorporate node importance across different layers. In these networks, defined by separate interconnected graphs without connections between different layers, the value of a node's centrality is determined by the sum of the values of the connected nodes within each specific layer, similar to traditional eigenvector centrality calculations. Unlike standard approaches, our approach takes into account the relationships between different network layers and their respective impact on the centrality values. Unlike current multi-layer eigenvector centrality frameworks that account for inter-layer connections, our approach uses a separate set of equations that can be solved using a hybrid algorithm. This new algorithm first solves a set of simplified equations based on the inter-layer connections, followed by a power method to solve the general eigenvector equations. We validate our approach by applying it to real-world datasets, including a dataset representing social media interactions among two distinct groups. Our analysis shows that networks defined by a single layer accurately replicate the results obtained from the full multi-layer network, and that our approach is particularly effective in identifying central nodes within certain groups by excluding "peripheral" nodes from specific layers. Our research also discovers that the degree of variation between different network layers affects the distribution of centrality values, with a 10% change in layer variation leading to a 6-8% change in the centrality value distribution. Moreover, by conducting a synthetic experiment, we find that our approach is capable of detecting central nodes even in networks defined by a single layer, and that the accuracy of these rankings correlates strongly with the actual network structure. Our method can be applied to a wide range of real-world problems involving multi-layered networks, such as analyzing economic transactions between different industries or identifying influential leaders within disparate social groups. Our approach is also compatible with weighted networks and provides a suitable alternative to existing methods by offering a clear and intuitive interpretation of the centrality values. This study investigates how spheres interact with water upon impact, specifically the process known as surface seal that occurs as the sphere enters the water's surface. This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes ("pinch-off time") generally hold for both slow-moving and fast-moving spheres, yet require further refinement, especially in the middle speed range. In fact, at mid-range speeds, pinch-off times relate differently to fluid dynamics than they do at either low or high speeds, indicating that increased pressures inside the formed cavity play a significant role. In addition, our findings include the shift from the deeper water-entrapment phenomenon to the surface-seal regime, and observations on the partial-seal, rippling-cavity-surface, and secondary pinch-off stages of water-entry interactions. A comprehensive discussion of existing and newly observed phenomena in the surface-seal regime is also presented. Moreover, our research includes an analytical model of the water-entry Pinch-off Time, Dynamics, and Entrapment Depth for the sphere water-entry interaction in the surface-seal regime. This analytical model of the sphere water-entry interaction incorporates both the slow, partially and fast, fully submerged water-entry stages, and it also includes a novel discussion of the 50 degree critical cavity-wall slope, commonly observed in both the slow and fast water-entry stages. This research was conducted using a high-speed, partially submerged water tank facility equipped with a precision velocity adjustment system and a three-dimensional, passive particle image velocimetry (3D PIV) measurement system. Our calculations using first-principles methods reveal that cubanite exhibits unusual orbital selectivity, with electrons occupying certain molecular orbitals while being localized in other atomic ones. This phenomenon is exceptionally rare in 3d transition metal compounds, providing a theoretical basis for the experimentally observed lack of charge disproportionation, anomalous Mössbauer spectra, and ferromagnetic coupling between adjacent iron ions. Moreover, our results predict that cubanite's electronic properties can change depending on its crystal structure, taking on either an orbital-selective Mott phase or an Mott-Hubbard phase, and that it may exhibit metal-to-insulator transitions triggered by structural changes or applied pressure. This predicted diversity of behavior makes cubanite a promising subject for future experimental and theoretical study, particularly using techniques that resonate with 57Fe nuclei. Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a more streamlined clinical approach that solely utilizes CT scans for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus with satisfactory precision. To achieve this, we designed an automatic, start-to-finish method based on deep neural networks called the Dilated Dense Attention Unet. This model leverages spatial and channel attention mechanisms in dense blocks to prioritize specific features and regions. It employs dilated convolutional layers to manage memory requirements and expand its ability to detect distant patterns. We gathered a comprehensive dataset consisting of 792 CT scans from 288 different patients with varied anatomies and included air pockets, feeding tubes, and proximal tumors. To test the robustness of our network, we conducted repeat studies on different training and validation sets. Our model produced a dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.79, a mean surface distance of 5.4 mm, and a Hausdorff distance of 14.7 mm for 287 test scans. These results demonstrate the efficacy of a simplified, CT-only clinical approach for identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus. Our code is available online at this link https://github.com/yousefis/DenseUnet_Esophagus_Segmentation.

Tantalum oxide compounds, with the formula Ta$_2$O$_5$, are distinguished by unique properties including high dielectric values and minimal reflectivity. Recent studies have also considered Ta$_2$O$_5$ nanoparticles as potential enhancers for hadron therapy treatments of cancer. To understand the material's electronic behavior, researchers have used theoretical simulations from first principles. Yet, Ta$_2$O$_5$ has various forms, complicating attempts to identify their individual features. To resolve this issue, researchers used time-dependent density functional methods to study the energy loss function in Ta$_2$O$_5$, specifically in its optical state, and across different polymorphs. These studies have demonstrated that experimental reflection loss signals can be interpreted assuming that Ta$_2$O$_5$'s $\gamma$-phase represents the primary structure of the material. Notably, researchers have also determined that both the effects of local fields and spin-orbit interactions are vital to correctly determining the energy loss of Ta$_2$O$_5$. Lastly, further validating the $\gamma$-Ta$_2$O$_5$ structure, researchers have used a Monte Carlo method to compare calculated reflection loss spectra with the actual results of experiments, achieving a very accurate match. Ultimately, this research has clarified the crystal structure of Ta$_2$O$_5$, and provides a method for predicting its electronic behavior in other situations. Additionally, by utilizing similar approaches, researchers believe that they can also understand the energy loss of other oxide compounds. Lastly, this study has utilized very advanced computational methods, involving simulations of 108 electrons using time-dependent density functional and Monte Carlo techniques.

Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors, such as information literacy, and social media influences, but ignored a third aspect: the impact of the physical separation of Americans in geographical regions. We tested the significance of this phenomenon, known as "The Big Sort," on online misinformation spread. We analyzed more than 8 million Reddit comments from news articles spanning four years and found that misinformation did not spread primarily through the features of the Reddit platform, but rather was linked to user population size in each state, following a supply-and-demand model. Furthermore, variations in misinformation dissemination were explained by local personality traits and cultural characteristics rather than economic, social, or political conditions. In areas where residents are less diligent in nature, and cultures place little emphasis on adherence to norms, we found increased circulation of all news, including credible sources. In contrast, areas with diligent and norm-adherent populations restricted misinformation circulation, but also limited access to credible news sources. Our study's findings were robust across different measurements of misinformation circulation and survived additional tests. We concluded that The Big Sort significantly contributes to the circulation of misinformation and suggested strategies to reduce its spread, such as targeting influential users who reside in areas with diligent populations. We also noted that further research is necessary to investigate interactions with other factors like personal characteristics and varying conditions within regions. Finally, we highlighted the importance of considering The Big Sort in studies of misinformation dissemination elsewhere in the world. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to augment a user's specific aspect preferences in each domain by transferring complementary preferences from other domains, while maintaining domain-specific uniqueness through adversarial training and dynamically determining the degree of complementarity using GAPE. Additionally, we introduce a Multi-Domain Adaptation Network (MDAN) to capture a user's general, domain-agnostic aspect preference. By integrating the domain-specific aspect preference and the domain-agnostic aspect preference, MSDCR attains a thorough understanding of user preferences across each data-poor domain. The empirical evaluations on real-world datasets unequivocally demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR over state-of-the-art single-domain and CDR models. The proposed approach also achieves meaningful interpretability results, enabling the degree of complementarity of user preferences across domains to be actionable, which is conducive to practical recommendations. The code for MSDCR is available at: https://github.com/zhoukai1997/MSDCR.

Convex optimization issues often take on a more manageable form when represented with conic formulations that leverage a wide variety of exotic cones. A correlation between this approach and the residual Hubble diagram values of Type Ia supernovae holds a $3.6\sigma$ significance and is consistent with dark matter effects due to galactic halos. Furthermore, we constrained galactic halo properties, including the mass-to-light ratio $\Gamma$ and the radial distribution of matter density within haloes $\rho(r)$. Based on this analysis, we formulated an equation to calculate the lens-induced additional random scattering in SN Ia magnitudes: $\sigma_{\rm lens} = (0.06 \pm 0.017) \cdot (d_{\rm C}(z)/ d_{\rm C}(1))^{3/2}$. As a result, the lens-induced apparent magnitude dispersion will approach the same magnitude as intrinsic SN Ia scatter at $z \approx 1.2$. Building upon this research, we propose an adjusted estimator for SN Ia distance moduli that incorporates the effects of lensing and is calculable using existing observational data, thereby potentially enhancing the precision of cosmological parameter inference from high-redshift SN Ia data. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted as part of bulk silicon studies, we demonstrate the consistent creation of high T center densities within the 220nm device layer of Silicon-On-Insulator (SOI) wafers, using a process that combines ion implantation and heat treatment. Unlike the case with the general linear group, however, these characteristics cannot be organized into a hierarchical structure. This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating the ability (or inability) of word2vec to effectively learn these structures. We also empirically assess the capabilities of these models using a substantial financial news dataset covering 12 years and spanning 42 million articles, relying on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists. Our results show that these models are prone to confusing antonyms as frequentist synonyms and mixing terms with opposing polarities. Notably, our research also uncovers the non-stationarity of financial corpora, revealing time-varying patterns in cosine similarity among polarized words or company names. Our analysis highlights the entangled mixture of semantic and co-occurring word distributions that these models are capturing, posing challenges for their disentanglement. Our work offers a mathematical framework that can be extended to unveil the underlying structures of various NLP embeddings, providing a precise theoretical understanding of how these models generate embeddings and offering a means of evaluating the quality of these embeddings. We also discuss various learning regret-based benchmarks that financial researchers can use to validate the quality of word2vec embeddings in specific contexts. Our research suggests that the cosine similarity alone is an inadequate metric for evaluating the performance of these models, given the complex interplay of semantic and distributional learning. Our analysis of financial corpora, combined with experiments using synthetic and real datasets, demonstrates that more sophisticated evaluation methods, such as learning regret-based benchmarks, are necessary to accurately assess the capabilities of these models. Our findings have implications for applications that rely on word2vec embeddings, particularly in contexts where the co-occurring distribution of terms is unstable or unpredictable, as seen in financial texts over extended periods. In multiagent learning settings beyond finding equilibria, learning rationalizable behavior that steers clear of dominated actions is another key goal. However, existing algorithms in the general multiplayer games scenario require an exponentially large number of samples relative to the number of players to determine rationalizable equilibria when working under bandit feedback. This research develops an initial suite of efficient algorithms to learn both Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE) and Correlated Equilibria (CE) that achieve polynomial sample complexities in line with problem parameters including the number of players. It also includes an enhanced approach for identifying a rationalizable action profile with a significantly improved sample requirement, exceeding the current benchmark established in 2021. Our innovative solutions involve the integration of multiple cutting-edge techniques that concurrently ensure the rationalizability and absence of (swap-)regret through correlated exploration and dynamic learning rate adjustments, offering potential value as standalone contributions. Moreover, our results are complemented by a sample complexity lower bound, underscoring the precision of the devised guarantees. This study is further distinguished by the incorporation of a rationalization-related performance gap term in the sample complexity lower bound, a novel aspect among multiagent learning setting research. Finally, our work is accompanied by a rationalizable CCE learning algorithm, enabling efficient determination of CCE without relying on the rationalization-by-learning-through-elimination approach introduced in 2020. This research is organized around the general multiplayer games setting and involves a specific variant called the multi-armed lottery game. In addition, we offer a rationalize-and-learn approach specifically tailored for the more constrained single-agent setting, which makes use of the existing single-agent research for rationalizability and swap-regret, thereby providing a more refined analysis of the underlying principles. This approach is distinguished by the integration of a dynamic learning rate and a stochastic rationalization procedure, resulting in a better characterization of the sample complexity required for rationalizable action selection. This characterizes the sample complexity under two different feedback mechanisms: passive observation of the opponent's actions and access to a teacher providing the best response to the player's current action. This leads to a better understanding of the underlying learning dynamics, which is further analyzed through the application of a new theorem relevant to the general context. This research is accompanied by an open problem involving the investigation of the underlying principles of the stochastic rationalization procedure used in the single-agent setting, which could be generalized to the multiagent context. While aligning the format of experimental data is a straightforward process, reconciling disparate theoretical predictions is a more complex task. Given the numerous contributors to different physical processes, with various inputs and outputs, incorporating the predictions requires significant integration efforts. Furthermore, since processes are often measured across a wide range of scales, evolution equations such as DGLAP need to be applied to PDF candidates or already precomputed in the outputs, necessitating a unified framework that can automate this process for the benefit of research groups working on PDF fitting and potential phenomenological studies. Such a framework is essential for optimizing time spent on theoretical predictions and ensuring consistency in PDF fitting. This paper outlines our theory pipeline's structure, particularly focusing on the integrations of (i) command-line tools, (i) code libraries, and (i) PDF fitting packages, as well as our approach to treating neutrino processes and incorporating the predictions of scattering off nuclear targets. To accelerate policy optimization in complex, dynamic systems with multiple influencing factors, reinforcement learning agents can effectively utilize previously collected historical data. Standard experience replay enables agents to retain information from prior iterations. However, the current approach equally values all collected observations, neglecting their varying significance. A more adaptive method, the variance reduction based experience replay framework, selectively leverages the most informative historical data. This approach prioritizes past observations more likely to represent the current target distribution. Theoretical and practical evaluations demonstrate that this method accelerates optimal policy discovery and boosts the effectiveness of state-of-the-art policy optimization methods. When compared to the conventional experience replay method, our proposed framework achieves a 10% to 30% reduction in the number of iterations required to converge. When applied to challenging, real-world systems like virtual characters and self-driving cars, this method yields 5% to 20% improvements in solution quality. The code is available at https://github.com/ChengXu98/VRBER.

In our analysis of conversational dialogue, we face numerous possible responses 
to any given history, leading us to present the MultiTalk Dataset. This large 
dataset comprises over 320,000 written conversational dialogue sentences, 
maintaining a high degree of complexity (a 10-way branching factor) along with 
6 conversation turns through strategically chosen continuation branches. Our study 
of dialogue generation involves multiple advancements, particularly in highly 
branching scenarios. To evaluate the diversity of generated text, we introduce a 
simple scoring algorithm grounded in bipartite graph matching, effectively 
incorporating various references. Our research spans multiple text generation 
tasks at various levels of conversational depth, utilizing text features derived 
automatically from pre-trained models. Ultimately, our primary challenge is a 
complex theory of mind problem that necessitates controlled text generation 
based on anticipated listener reactions. Our work in this area is notable for its 
difficulty, as evidenced by the meager 4% score achieved by our best model 
on this hard task. Our findings, datasets, and tools are available at: https://github.com/google-research-multilingual/MultiTalk.

We introduce MG-GLAM, a computational tool developed to rapidly create comprehensive N-body simulations for various cosmological theories, specifically modified gravity models. This program builds upon the existing GLAM code and incorporates an advanced multigrid method to solve the non-linear equations characteristic of modified gravity theories, resulting in highly efficient simulations. For $f(R)$ gravity, MG-GLAM includes multiple variations that mimic distinct behaviors of these models and offers tailored algorithms to maintain speed and precision. The code excels at producing a broad spectrum of modified gravity simulations and offers significant computational benefits, outperforming existing N-body simulations by a factor of over a hundred while yielding accurate results for key cosmological metrics. MG-GLAM is suited for creating large sets of modified gravity simulations that can be utilized in mock galaxy catalogues and emulators for ongoing and future galaxy surveys. The code is available for download at [www.mgglam.com].

Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal equivalence. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This paper develops Gaussian free field-valued processes in the upper half-plane and the first orthant of the complex plane, establishing their connection to multiple SLE evolving in time on these domains. We demonstrate that such connections can be made locally by driving multiple SLE with the Dyson model on the real line and the Bru-Wishart process on the positive reals, respectively. Ultimately, these pairings yield domains that evolve in time and associated Gaussian free fields. We observe their relationship to multiple SLE and, in the stationary setting, recover the results of Dan-Seppalainen-Weiss, the statistics of the Dyson model and the Bru-Wishart process, the asymptotic behavior of the imaginary surface in the stationary setting, and the relationship between the Bru-Wishart process and the BES process. Additionally, our findings enable us to couple multiple SLE in the upper half-plane and the first orthant, obtaining domains that evolve in time and associated Gaussian free fields. We demonstrate the compatibility of this coupling with the domain mark process of multiple SLE in the upper half-plane and the half-plane SLE with the radial loop measure in the first orthant. Finally, our approach allows us to characterize the fields associated with multiple SLE in the upper half-plane and the first orthant, ending with an open problem regarding the description of these fields. Our work builds upon the approach introduced in the paper by Miller and Sheffield, the results of Dan-Seppalainen-Weiss, the statistics of the Dyson model and the Bru-Wishart process, the asymptotic behavior of the imaginary surface in the stationary setting, the relationship between the Bru-Wishart process and the BES process, the compatibility of RLE with the radial loop measure, the results of Nagasa, the description of the fields associated with half-plane SLE with the radial loop measure, and the paper by Sheffield. Our work also includes an open problem regarding the description of these fields. Our paper is part of the collection named Papers from the MSRI program on Random Conformal Field Theory.

MediaWiki's 'WorkingWiki' is an open-source extension that converts a wiki
into a sophisticated collaborative platform for developing high-quality manuscripts
and software projects. Originally developed at McMaster University's theoretical
biology lab, WorkingWiki enables multiple users to work together on a range of
tasks by utilizing command-line tools to translate raw'source code' into desired outputs.
Its features cater specifically to programmers and researchers who use languages
like R, Python, and C, and it boasts specialized tools for seamless LaTeX editing.
By integrating features from collaborative editors, development environments,
version control systems, and publishing platforms, WorkingWiki unlocks the
full potential of wiki-based collaboration, and its customizable'makefiles'
and modular architecture enable users to tailor and repurpose its functionality. Though
developed in-house to suit McMaster University's particular needs, WorkingWiki
is now available to the broader public, awaiting the contributions of its potential users
who can further develop the project and extract its value from their own research.

Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of stellar mass black holes in the region. A crucial aspect of the theory that these sources are actually black holes is the claim that neutron star binaries with low masses exhibit recurring X-ray bursts within short intervals. This study contradicts that idea by revealing that about half of the known LMXBs, featuring a neutron star as the primary component, exhibit outburst recurrence times exceeding a decade when detected by the MAXI telescope. This study's findings also examine the likely distribution of recurrence times for newly discovered variables among the neutron star binaries with visible outbursts and finds that about 40% of these variables have the second longest recurrence times (a month to a year). Improving neural conversational agents' ability to produce diverse, engaging responses in casual conversations is a challenge. To tackle this issue, this paper introduces two significant innovations. Firstly, it proposes a new assessment metric that employs Natural Language Inference to gauge the semantic variety of responses generated by the model in a conversation. Using a previously established framework, this metric was tested and showed a clear connection between Natural Language Inference Diversity and semantic variety. It was discovered that the contradiction relation yields more precise results than the neutral relation in measuring diversity and integrating the NLI model's confidence achieves the highest performance to date. Secondly, this paper demonstrates a way to enhance the semantic variety of responses generated by the model through an iterative procedure called Diversity Threshold Generation, which, in comparison to standard generation methods, results in an average 137% improvement in NLI Diversity. Moreover, this method was integrated into a renowned conversational agent evaluation metric and discovered that Diversity Threshold Generation also leads to a 57% improvement in the similarity between responses. Finally, this paper's findings have been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/PranavTyagi/NLI_Diversity.

Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings levels to maintain the visualization's clarity. In contrast, an approach has been developed to remove edge crossings by splitting specific nodes, targeting the minimum number required to yield an edge-free (planar) drawing. The question of determining if an edge-free representation exists after breaking at most a specified number of nodes remains tractable in relation to that number. The paper presents an iterative bidding algorithm that achieves this level of tractability. The time spent by this algorithm is proportional to the number of nodes times the number of node splits. The problem of bipartite drawing after node splitting is known to be computationally hard, yet a recent study demonstrated its membership in the class of problems easily solved in time proportional to the number of nodes times the number of node splits, thereby improving the previous result of Proskinejad, Haghanoae, Efrim, and Eades, who had achieved a similar outcome using a more complex approach. The current algorithmic solution is significantly faster and provides the basis for a more economical heuristic used to break nodes progressively, aiming to minimize edge crossings without the constraint of complete planarity. The issue of finding the minimum number of node splits required for an edge-free representation remains harder, as evidenced by the recent study of Bannhi, Proskinejad, Haghanoae, Efrim, and Eades, who demonstrated its membership in the class of problems easily solved in time proportional to the number of nodes times the number of node splits. The current algorithm allows for a faster solution to this problem by comparing the number of splits in the easy solution with the number obtained in the hard solution, and infers the difficulty of the problem from the difference between these two numbers. The algorithmic approach provides the foundation for a number of possible variations, including a more intricate one that addresses the harder version of the problem. The paper also presents a number of possible benchmarks, featuring both synthetic and real-world data, and comparing its performance with the existing approach on these benchmarks shows that the new algorithm delivers superior outcomes in terms of execution time and node splits, while also achieving better results in terms of the number of edge crossings in comparison with the existing approach of Hagh

This paper will present our approach to optimizing bipedal robot walking assisted by thrusters using a closed-loop feedback system. By assuming that supervisory controllers are properly set, we will concentrate on refining joint trajectories to meet specific performance requirements. To achieve this, we will create a mediator filter utilizing reference governors to ensure that performance constraints are met. Due to the impacts and adjustments made during the gait cycle causing deviations from desired periodic orbits, we will ensure robust hybrid invariance through the application of predictive methods within a short timeframe. To maintain hybrid invariance, we will leverage the distinctive features of our model, the thrusters, to our advantage. The key benefit of our approach is that unlike other optimization-based nonlinear control methods, performance-related constraints are met during the single-support phase without reliance on costly numerical methods. Furthermore, the proposed thruster-assisted gait control framework allows for the utilization of performance and robustness-enhancing capabilities during particular phases of the gait cycle, a previously unreported aspect. The efficacy of our approach will be demonstrated through simulated tests of a hexapod robot. Due to the limited availability of data, a quadruped robot test case is presented in the discussion section. The code and the associated documentation can be accessed at: https://github.com/srosales/thruster-assisted-gait.

Becker-Denef-Lipschitz first observed in 1979 that over finite fields $k$, the total residue map $\text{res}$ from Laurent series to $k$ is expressible in a specific language, provided $t$ is included as a parameter. This discovery motivated further research into the properties of a specific mathematical theory related to valued fields. In the course of these investigations, the authors proved that this theory does not have a certain desirable feature and demonstrated that, for infinite fields $k$, the associated power series fields cannot be computationally decided. This, in turn, led to an analogous undecidability conclusion for a specific complex-valued field of power series. This paper presents an enhanced version of this undecidability result, as well as an analysis of a particular algebraic property shared by the constants of these power series fields. Additionally, the authors explore two specific generalizations of this predictability phenomenon for more versatile fields of power series. This field of research is further connected to another celebrated undecidability result related to exponential fields, as shown in the paper's appendix. This work builds upon the results obtained in the course of an earlier investigation focused on recursive algebraic geometry. The authors' research was previously published in the form of an arXiv preprint, where it received a notable amount of attention, with particular interest shown by the mathematical logic and theoretical computer science communities. This current version of the paper includes minor revisions aimed at clarifying certain proofs and improving the presentation of the results, as well as an introduction to the research and an appendix containing a relevant context. This work has been accepted for presentation at the conference titled Minds and Machines at the University of Michigan, as well as at the conference titled Logic and Computability in Russia. This paper's results have also been presented at university talks given at the University of California, Berkeley, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Harvard University, the University of Wisconsin-Madison, and the University of Chicago. This paper is dedicated to the memory of its second author's father, Dr. Abraham Lipschitz, who passed away in March 2022. This research was supported by award number CCF-2016158 and award number CCF-1813219, as well as an NSF Graduate Research Fellowship awarded to its first author. We investigate the concept of coordination through strategic decision-making, focusing on a scenario where agents select between two tasks of varying difficulty that are randomly distributed and partially known. It has been found that a stable state of cooperation, characterized by a straightforward linear pattern, can be achieved when there is a wide range of possible task difficulties. Furthermore, it was discovered that the most advantageous action for each agent in response to an approachable strategy profile can be complex and nonlinear when the distribution of task difficulties is not uniform. A computational method has been established to calculate a cooperative equilibrium through learning within the set of linear policy options. It was also found that coordinating agents can benefit from sharing partial information about the task distribution, and that this improves the efficiency of cooperation to a significant degree. In addition, an operationally feasible approach has been developed to coordinate agents in a system where tasks are repeatedly generated and partially known. This approach combines learning, cooperative equilibrium, and partial information sharing, and it leads to cooperation that is not only stable but also increasingly efficient over time. This has been demonstrated in extensive simulations conducted using a regular network of robots. It was further found that in cases where tasks are consistently and easily accessible, cooperation systems based on random search can rely on a simple linear pattern to optimize their performance. This has implications for the design of efficient coordination systems based on learning and partial information sharing, especially when they are limited in their computational and communication capabilities. This has been illustrated in a scenario where robots are gathering data from airborne sensors. Based on how entities cooperate, FL can be categorized into two primary forms - horizontal and vertical FL. The former involves participants who collaborate using identical data attributes, while in the latter, entities with overlapping sample IDs collaborate using different features. Although this design has been previously proposed, we highlight a key variation where the end mirrors are optically linked to form an additional resonating cavity, offering a more flexible design where the detector could transition between this configuration and the conventional signal-recycled Michelson setup in response to changing environmental conditions. We also explore the effect of this design on the detector's sensitivity in various conditions and offer possible ways to enhance sensitivity further. A question remains regarding the secondary component of GW190814 - whether it's a neutron star or a black hole of minimal mass. Researchers have introduced an energy density functional, named BigApple, which accurately matches the neutron star's mass of 2.60 solar masses and is in line with GW190814's data. By utilizing BigApple along with four well-established relativistic mean-field forces, a study delves into the characteristics of finite nuclei, nuclear matter, and neutron stars. The predicted properties of finite nuclei and calculated quantities of nuclear matter align well with empirical and experimental values, demonstrating the BigApple parameter set's reliability. Notably, BigApple successfully matches GW190814's data for canonical tidal deformability, while the dimensionless moment of inertia falls within the estimated range based on PSR J0737-3039A's analysis. Furthermore, BigApple predicts a characteristic oscillation mode frequency in neutron stars, consistent with predictions derived from PSR J0346+0241's mass and radius estimation. Overall, the BigApple parameter set proves a suitable tool for investigating dense matter properties, offering specific predictions that align with observations and constraints. These predictions include a maximum mass of 2.60 solar masses for neutron stars, a radius of 12.5 km for a 1.4 solar mass neutron star, and a moment of inertia of 15.7 km^2 for a 1.4 solar mass neutron star. Additionally, BigApple predicts a tidal heat flux peak in massive neutron star binaries, and a characteristic oscillation mode frequency in neutron stars that could be tested with gravitational waves or electromagnetic observations. The BigApple energy density functional also predicts a transition from the neutron star phase to black holes at high densities, characterized by a first-order phase transition to a non-zero proton fraction. This predicts a sharp boundary for the neutron star phase, and a prolate neutron star configuration in the density range where this phase exists. Lately, researchers have focused intensely on solid electronic theory's strongly correlated systems and graphene, yet the $sp^{2}$-electrons that form Dirac bands in graphene lack strong interactions. Consequently, novel, interaction-induced phenomena tied to Dirac points are underutilized. We propose GaCu$_{3}$(OH)$_{6}$Cl$_{2}$ as a new material where Dirac electrons are paired with strong interactions and frustrated magnetism. Calculations indicate its crystallographic and electronic properties harbor symmetry-protected Dirac points at the Fermi level, allowing for multifaceted physics encompassing possible instabilities of charge, magnetism, or superconductivity. By merging various methods to assess its many-body behavior, researchers have observed potential transitions to Mott-Hubbard, magnetic or charge ordering states, along with $f$-wave unconventional superconductivity in this unique compound. Despite its complexity, researchers believe GaCu$_{3}$(OH)$_{6}$Cl$_{2}$ can be synthesized, and its study holds significant potential for advancing understanding of interplay between different interactions in solid state physics. Neural language models have largely surpassed $N$-gram models due to better performance, but our findings suggest that $n$-gram models still excel in many situations with low computational costs, demonstrating a strong foundation of language understanding. Building upon this discovery, we developed a neural model that learns from the remaining knowledge between $n$-gram models and the true language distribution, allowing for both a deeper grasp of language and the flexibility to adjust models through the $n$-gram base without altering the neural model. Through extensive experiments on tasks including language modeling, machine translation, and summarization, our hybrid approach consistently delivers enhanced performance over standard neural models and facilitates seamless domain adaptation by simply swapping the $n$-gram base, eliminating the need for additional training. In an inflationary model, with a specific type of $\alpha$-attractor potential, we examine the behavior in the high-$k$ regime, where cosmological perturbations exhibit excessive growth and negative values of the Bardeen potential. This regime facilitates the formation of primordial black holes (PBHs). Our calculations were carried out within a spatially flat gauge with a non-zero fluctuation in the inflaton field and its impact on the background gravitational field. We determined the scalar density fluctuations ($\sigma$), asymmetry ($\beta$), and PBH mass fraction ($f_\mathrm{PBH}$) in relation to specific mass scales. Our results reveal the formation of PBHs over the $k$ range $0.43\times 10^{13}$ Mpc$^{-1}$ to $9.8\times 10^{13}$ Mpc$^{-1}$, with corresponding mass ranges and properties. These predictions align with forecasts from LISA and other gravitational wave detectors, with a significant overlap in the $f_\mathrm{PBH}$ estimates. Furthermore, our analysis implies that PBH formation might be a ubiquitous consequence of scalar perturbations in inflationary cosmology. Our findings also support the use of PBH formation as a means of detecting the high-$k$ regime in the cosmic microwave background, specifically targeting regions with particular properties. Our potential approaches to confirming these predictions, and analyzing the high-$k$ regime in general, include utilizing CMB, LISA, and other detectors in relation to the $f_\mathrm{PBH}$ estimates. Our results provide a foundational understanding for investigating the high-$k$ regime and its connection to PBH formation, with implications that can be applied to a variety of inflationary models. Our code is available upon request.

A key factor for maintaining stability in future low-carbon power grids is expected to be energy storage systems. Studies examining past experiences reveal a common issue with storage units - they frequently fail to take advantage of high-price signals during periods of low energy supply. This behavior has been often attributed to inaccurate forecasting or operational issues. However, our research suggests a more plausible explanation is rooted in risk-averse decision-making practices. Utilizing a stochastic self-scheduling approach and real data from the Australian electricity market, our findings show that risk-conscious storage units prioritize short-term cost savings by engaging in local price speculation, and tend to ignore opportunities in periods with unusual price fluctuations. This has significant policy implications, given the difficulty of detecting and managing storage units' risk aversion. Moreover, it highlights the risk of storage units contributing to market instability rather than reducing it. This study also highlights the difference in behavior between different types of storage units, with some being more prone to risk aversion than others. This information can be used by market regulators to develop more effective strategies for managing storage units' risk aversion and promoting healthier market behavior. Furthermore, it provides an important lesson for storage unit operators on the risks of extreme price behavior and the importance of properly valuing risk in their decision-making processes. This research was conducted using real data and scenarios from the Australian electricity market, but its findings are likely applicable to other markets with similar characteristics. This includes markets that are decentralized, subject to price fluctuations, and feature risk-averse storage units. By utilizing the code's efficiency to handle computational demands, exchange interaction effects, valley distribution, and electron distribution were examined in a range of positions, orientations, and under applied electric fields. The findings are displayed in an interactive format that shows donor placement's impact on the behavior of valley and orbital components. The research yields a practical understanding and accurate prediction of necessary conditions to execute reliable two-qubit operations with silicon-based quantum processors. The proposed approach has been tested by comparing theoretical predictions with experimental data on the hyperfine structure of silicon donor arrays and the influence of electric fields on the behavior of spin Qubits. The findings have been validated by conducting a range of calculations that analyze the efficiency of the model in predicting configuration interaction effects. The code has been made available for public use as a useful tool for researchers working with quantum processors based on silicon donors. The proposed research has been conducted by the author alone, with support from the University of Warwick. The institution has copyright and ownership rights of the code and research findings. The development of the code was funded by the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council (EPSRC). The research was conducted as part of the SiQuOR project, a collaborative effort between the University of Warwick, University of Cambridge, and University College London. The project aims to address the challenge of coupled donor technology, with a specific focus on valley degeneracy, motion-induced decoherence, and array-based data storage. The research has been published in the journal npj Quantum Information, under the title "Full configuration interaction simulations of exchange-coupled donors in silicon using multi-valley effective mass theory". The associated pre-print has been made available for public access on the arXiv server. The research has also been presented at the Quantum Computing and Simulation Workshop, held in Bristol, UK, at the SiQuOR Project Meeting, held in London, UK, and at the Quantum Technologies Workshop, held in Cambridge, UK. Our investigation focused on the transport properties of HgTe quantum wells near their critical thickness, where the energy gap is minimal, and the energy spectrum is described by a singular Dirac cone structure. Both large and small-sized (mesoscopic) samples were examined as part of this study. When looking at small-sized samples, a well-defined, quantized resistance emerged at low magnetic field strength due to Landau filling, and was closely related to helical edge states that form around the neutral point of the samples. Conversely, larger samples showed significant resistance oscillations in low-magnetic-field conditions. This behavior is attributed to interaction between the neutral state at the edge and a non-neutral hole Landau level within the bulk material. A hypothetical model incorporating a reservoir formed by heavy holes has been developed as an explanatory framework. This model highlights the importance of magnetic field-induced coupling between this reservoir and the free Dirac-like electrons in the bulk material. Consequently, a distinctive return of the resistance to its non-magnetic value was observed once the neutral state within the bulk material is achieved with increasing magnetic field. This phenomenon has been examined across a range of sample sizes, examining the fundamental requirements necessary for neutral state coupling and resulting resistance oscillations. A comparative analysis with theoretical transport models based on a semi-circle distribution of edge state energy has been performed, and examined in the context of growth conditions and sample geometry. This has provided valuable insights into the examination of edge state and bulk state interaction across a range of material widths. The examination of both small and large-sized samples has revealed the intricate relationship between transport properties, edge and bulk state interaction, and the resulting spatial and energetic distribution of the Dirac-like electrons. This complex relationship is a key consideration for the appropriate utilization of HgTe quantum wells in the development of future quantum computing and quantum transport technology. A comprehensive understanding of the energy gap, coupled with examination of the energy spectrum, has also been gained from this investigation. The examination of small-sized samples has revealed a discrete, quantized energy spectrum in the low-magnetic-field condition, whereas examination of large-sized samples has revealed a continuous, coupled distribution in the low-magnetic-field condition. In Dynamic Time-Division Duplexing (TDD), individual cells can schedule uplink and downlink modes independently, depending on local traffic conditions, but this causes interference between neighboring cells, turning a critical problem into an NP-hard mixed-integer non-convex challenge. We've developed an efficient and localized solution, separating power allocation and scheduling processes, first assigning power independently to cells, followed by a non-cooperative game determining scheduling modes, with payoffs calculated according to the level of interference and required cell communication. Simulations, set in an outdoor scenario with multiple small cells, reveal our method outperforms static TDD solutions. Additionally, we find that in low-load scenarios, a more conservative scheduling approach is ideal, whereas in highly congested areas, a more aggressive strategy is preferable. In all cases, our method delivers significant improvements over static TDD solutions. Moreover, we discover that in scenarios with balanced uplink and downlink traffic, a symmetric scheduling approach leads to better outcomes than more aggressive, asymmetric strategies. Lastly, we conclude that in 5G Dynamic TDD systems, the exclusive ownership of scheduling modes can result in significant performance gains, exceeding 30% in certain cases. Nonetheless, this finding is subject to change based on specific system configurations and applications. Lastly, we propose a new, lucrative application for dynamic TDD, involving a "scheduling mode market" that allows cells to trade their scheduling permissions with each other, presenting both convex and non-convex versions of this complex problem. Lastly, we outline potential future adaptation and expansion of this innovative idea, including integrating other mobile system parameters, conducting thorough load simulations, exploring alternative pricing mechanisms, and examining the economic and efficiency implications of this scheduling market. In this work, we introduce a novel meta-learning framework centered on ODE neural networks, which acquires an understanding of gradients. This framework grants optimizers enhanced flexibility and infuses an automatic inductive bias into tasks, as we have found. Through the simplest Hamiltonian Neural Network implementation, our method proves more effective than a comparable LSTM-based meta-learner for a simulated task and MNIST with ReLU activations in the model being optimized, as well as consistently outperforming traditional optimization techniques for the artificial task and delivering results on par with standard optimization for MNIST. Nonetheless, more complex HNN models fail to match the baseline for MNIST. Our framework also yields theoretical insights, as we determine that its performance is directly tied to the accuracy with which its latent state mirrors the target distribution following the initial conditioning. Our work is concluded by outlining potential paths for improving our framework, as we believe there are numerous exciting developments to be made within the realm of baseline HNN meta-learning. Our code has been made publicly available at https://github.com/ghalegh.

Simply enhancing a machine learning model's accuracy is not sufficient, as we must also focus on increasing its reliability. This consideration is crucial for creating robust AI systems that are capable of withstanding critical situations in areas like transportation, finance, and medical fields. We recommend developing a collaborative multi-agent framework that combines artificial intelligence with human input. This proposed system involves two key components: a scoring agent that calculates a reliability metric for each prediction, penalizing both overoptimistic and overly cautious results; and a refinement agent that utilizes a set of human-defined safety guidelines to identify and rectify unusual instances. It then uses these corrected examples to update its model through transfer learning. We put the proposed system through testing on datasets modified to contain artificial errors and found that it effectively improves both the accuracy and reliability of the model with only a limited increase in training data. This approach can be applied to any machine learning model, and we demonstrate its effectiveness using models developed for a specific application. This proposed human-in-the-loop online multi-agent framework can be used to enhance the reliability of machine learning models in a wide range of situations. This approach is particularly effective in areas like transportation and medicine, where the consequences of developing a false sense of trust in AI systems could be severe. A newly defined polynomial, referred to as the nth toroidal colored Jones polynomial, is established for links in a thickened torus. Dubbed $J_n^T$, this polynomial demonstrates numerous properties similar to the original colored Jones polynomial, and notably displays volume conjecture behavior. By applying $J_n^T$, we prove the volume conjecture holds true for a specific link, and provide computational data suggesting it holds for additional links. Moreover, $J_n^T$ can be represented through two distinct constructions, a pseudo-operator invariant, and a construction rooted in the Kauffman bracket skein module of the torus. Notably, $J_n^T$ yields invariants for virtual and biperiodic links, providing an instance of volume conjecture behavior in a virtual link. Lastly, $J_n^T$ can be defined using combinatorial operations on volume representations, offering a potential approach to testing the volume conjecture. The most substantial links covered in this study include the toroidal Grassmannian links, a specific class of links with planar projections, and a particular type of biperiodic links formed through the closure of biperiodic knots. The volumes of these links converge to the values predicted by $J_n^T$, in accordance with the volume conjecture. The proposed construction of $J_n^T$ also yields invariants for links in certain non-compact spaces, specifically the Euclidean space and the Riemannian manifold, demonstrating volume conjecture behavior in these settings. The relationship between $J_n^T$ and the Aichi-Kauffman polynomial of links in the 4-dimensional Euclidean space is established through a volume change formula, and the derivative of $J_n^T$ is found to be equivalent to the colored volume polynomial of links in the 4-dimensional Euclidean space, with the notation that the derivative operation is defined combinatorially. The proposed construction of $J_n^T$ also yields invariants for links in the complex projective space, providing an instance of volume conjecture behavior in a complex setting. The primary objective of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Advances in deep learning, specifically utilizing BERT, have led to significant progress in this area, with several strategies being developed to combine structured knowledge for enhanced performance.  Additionally, multiple data augmentation techniques have been discovered to be valuable tools in natural language processing tasks.  Building on prior work incorporating BERT and WordNet knowledge, this study explores various data augmentation techniques in context-gloss pairs to enhance the efficacy of WSD.  Experimental results indicate that both sentence and word-level augmentation strategies are effective in addressing WSD, while the incorporation of hypernyms' definitions from a lexical knowledge base can further improve performance.  A comparative analysis of different context-gloss augmentation techniques is conducted, revealing that the application of back translation to definitions produces the most satisfactory outcomes.  A modulated model incorporating the most successful augmentation technique is then developed to provide a benchmark for comparative evaluation of future approaches.  This study is relevant to a broad range of applications involving the utilization of a lexical knowledge base, including but not limited to text summarization, information extraction, and natural language generation.  The code and model are available for public access at https://github.com/zwang93/Word-Sense-Disambiguation.

The CMS experiment at the CERN LHC detected the production of top quarks for the first time using proton-lead data at an 8.16 TeV nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy. Top quark production was identified in events featuring one isolated electron or muon and four or more jets, from a data set totaling 174 inverse nanobarns of luminosity. The measured signal exceeded the five-standard-deviation threshold expected for a background-only hypothesis, and the cross-sectional measurement for top quark pairs was found to be 45 nanobarns with an 8-nanobarn uncertainty, consistent with theoretical predictions from quantum chromodynamics. This finding was further confirmed by analyzing data sets totaling 15 inverse nanobarns of luminosity at two different energy settings, an 8.16 TeV and a 5.02 TeV nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy. The measured cross-sectional values for both energies aligned with theoretical predictions from quantum chromodynamics, and the ratio of wide-angle hadron production to electron/muon tags was determined to be around one. The observed top quark production marked the initial detection of this process in proton-nucleus collisions and contributed significantly to the understanding of nuclear matter via top quark studies. The measurement also paved the way for investigating top quark-mediated processes in proton-nucleus collisions. The data and resulting analysis tools have value beyond top quark research, given the large amount of proton-lead data at the LHC. The research was based on findings from a 2015 data collection. This study focuses on key elements in cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing, specifically schema linking and value filling. To enhance encoding abilities, a column selection auxiliary task is proposed, leveraging explicit targets for relevance matching. Additionally, two value filling approaches are presented to bridge the gap between current zero-shot parsers and practical applications, considering that many existing parsers overlook value filling in synthesized SQL. Experiments on the Spider dataset demonstrate the superiority of our proposed framework over baseline models in terms of execution and exact set match accuracy when database contents are inaccessible, with further analysis pointing to areas for future improvement. Moreover, our proposed framework shows promising performance when database contents are accessible, with results showing potential for enhancing existing state-of-the-art models. All proposed approaches are evaluated and demonstrated through accessible database text-to-SQL examples. The code is available at https://github.com/ghrua/SpiderZero.

This paper delves into the utilization of differential privacy within the framework of graph-based data. It outlines the DP formulations relevant to publishing graphs, statistical analysis associated with graphs, and machine learning on graph-based data, including graph neural networks. However, applying DP to graph data poses significant challenges due to interconnected data points that can form complex relationships. This issue is compounded by a lack of universally accepted DP formulation in graph-based contexts. This problem further exacerbates the difficulty in conducting private machine learning on graph data. A notable absence of systematised research on graph-based learning in relation to privacy was a key driver of our work, leading us to explore various formulations of DP on graphs, discuss associated challenges and promising applications including GNNs. This work also compares and distinguishes different graph-based learning tasks from those that incorporate graph neural networks. Ultimately, our work is concluded by examining open research questions and exploring possible avenues for further investigation in this domain.
