We introduce the G4C challenge, focusing on how natural language interactions can be guided by set objectives, which can be evaluated through the lens of a role-playing game. Specifically, we select Dungeons and Dragons as our testing ground. Within this framework, player characters represent learners with distinct identities, while the Dungeon Master functions as both a guide and authority figure tasked with leading them toward a common goal. Our methodology combines a theory-of-mind-inspired approach with reinforcement learning, training a Dungeon Master that: first learns to anticipate the players' responses to its dialogue based on past D&D conversations, then utilizes these predictions to assess the effectiveness of its guidance, which in turn propels the players toward a collective goal. Human assessments alongside automated testing reveal that a Dungeon Master trained through reinforcement learning to consider a theory-of-mind of the players enhances their ability to achieve shared objectives rooted within their shared world context. Our findings are open to the public as the first release of the G4C dataset, which includes text and intentional representations depicting a dynamic, co-created world. Our framework is available at https://github.com/udc/. Our work is a response to the long-standing challenge of creating effective and automatic learning guides, as well as the burgeoning interest in incorporating a theory-of-mind in AI systems. We believe that guiding learning through narrative experiences offers a novel approach to this problem, while incorporating a theory-of-mind enhances the realism of Dungeons and Dragons as well as similar educational scenarios. We propose several possible applications of our dataset for the community, ranging from evaluating learning guides to providing a platform for creative storytelling. Lastly, we outline possible pathways for future development, including the integration of role-playing game theory and learning guides based on natural language inference. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/udc/. The intricate relationship between protein knots and their folding processes is an area that biologists are actively trying to grasp. Recent research categorizes the spatial arrangements of knotted proteins using advanced topological models. A novel statistical approach, inspired by topological principles, enables the comparison of knotted protein structures based on their spatial projections. This analysis uncovers the distinctions in geometry among proteins with trefoil knots and also identifies clustering patterns according to their sequence similarities. By focusing on the intrinsic properties of these proteins in their natural state, our research uncovers various folding pathways for trefoil knots and reveals that proteins with shallow knots follow a distinct pathway compared to those with deep knots. Specifically, this study finds that proteins with shallow knots adopt a double-loop structure before folding, in contrast to proteins with deep knots that were previously found to exhibit different folding patterns. This finding is further validated through molecular dynamics simulations. The statistical approach also allows for the comparison of folding pathways among proteins with the same knot type, revealing different patterns among them. This is demonstrated by identifying differences between folding pathways of trefoil knots found in proteins that contain hydrophobic and ionic interactions. The statistics used in this research are uniquely suited for examining the folding processes of biopolymers and can be applied to the study of other knotted proteins, as well as biopolymers such as DNAs and proteins with knot-like structures formed through external forces. The method used here for comparing the intrinsic properties of knotted proteins can be combined with other statistical approaches, such as cluster analysis and machine learning, and can be applied to the study of other complex systems that involve spatial arrangements and internal components, including financial transactions, social networks, and the structures of molecules. The general framework of this statistics framework involves topological projections, persistence diagrams, and the comparison of persistent diagrams using the distance metric called the Wasserstein distance, which can be simplified as the number of trefoil knots on a sphere by counting the number of loops and the number of intersections between them. Nonetheless, the scale and variety of such counterfactual data are restricted when sourced from crowds and become costly to extend to new perturbation types when produced through supervised methods. To address these challenges, we present a novel framework called DISCO that generates high-quality counterfactual data at a large scale automatically. This framework prompts a general-purpose large language model to generate phrasal alterations, while a task-specific instructor model culls high-quality examples from the generated pool. We demonstrate that employing this counterfactual data in learning yields a relatively compact model that exhibits a 6% boost in robustness and 5% gain in distributional generalizability when evaluated against various rigorous metrics. Moreover, this model is 15% more adept at distinguishing genuine and counterfactual instances, as shown in evaluations conducted through both human-generated and human-AI collaborative settings. Ultimately, counterfactual data of this kind at a large scale also enables seamless extension to novel perturbation types, thereby expanding its utility to other tasks. The code for this project is now publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/nyu-algorithms/disco.

Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. Many instances are instead attributed to contaminants between graphene and the substrate, or alternative processes such as van der Waals epitaxy. This study discovered that when growing the Heusler compound GdPtSb on clean graphene substrates, it results in a unique 30 degree rotated superstructure, not explicable through other mechanisms. This rotation domain percentage significantly increases at lower growth temperatures. It's suggested that slower surface diffusion at lower temperatures favors the remote epitaxial process over faster surface diffusion at higher temperatures. Moreover, this study demonstrated that precise annealing of the graphene and consideration of film/substrate lattice mismatches are necessary for achieving epitaxial relationships with a range of Heusler compounds, including LaPtSb and GdAuGe. The distinctive 30 degree rotated superstructure offers a potential experimental signature for identifying remote epitaxy. If successfully harnessed, this process could lead to the creation of complex oxide heterostructures with unique properties, facilitating the reuse of expensive substrate materials and reducing production costs. The specific case of GdPtSb highlights the versatility of this approach, as it results in coexistence of different epitaxial relationships between individual grains, yet remote epitaxy itself was confirmed through theoretical modeling. Conditional GANs have demonstrated superior performance in tasks requiring the generation of specific classes.  However, creating training data with multiple labels to control multiple conditions simultaneously proves impractical due to the extensive annotation required, a problem that limits the availability of such datasets in real-world applications.  This paper investigates a new setting called the single positive scenario, in which each piece of data is marked by only a single relevant label without any additional information regarding potential irrelevant labels.  A novel technique known as single-to-multi-label sampling was developed to generate multi-label data based on this single positive label annotation.  This new approach is a supplemental tool that allows current unconditional and conditional GANs to generate high-quality multi-label data while significantly reducing the required annotation. Experimental findings with real image datasets demonstrate that the technique can effectively produce accurate multi-label data even in comparison to a model trained using comprehensive datasets.  The technique's applicability to real-world applications is demonstrated through the reconstruction of medical reports along with the generation of movie recommendations.  The code for this paper is available at https://github.com/lingeze/Single2Multi.

The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and wristbands allows users to easily access health data including activity levels, sleep patterns, and sports history. Successful smart healthcare relies on training machine learning models using a large quantity of user data, but several key challenges arise. Primarily, user data exists in disparate segments, complicating data aggregation without breaching privacy protocols. Secondly, models trained on cloud platforms struggle to accommodate personalization requirements. This paper introduces FedHealth, a pioneering federated transfer learning framework for wearable healthcare designed to address these difficulties. FedHealth aggregates data via federated learning and employs transfer learning to develop personalized models. It succeeds in providing accurate, personalized healthcare without compromising security and data confidentiality. Experimentation reveals that FedHealth yields 5.3% greater accuracy in wearable activity recognition when compared to conventional approaches. Furthermore, FedHealth demonstrates versatility, extensibility, and vast potential applications in the healthcare industry. The framework serves as a foundational module for developing complex healthcare models, a critical discovery for the healthcare industry. The framework and its underlying code are available for public use at this link: https://github.com/ghru/FedHealth.

Our design leverages this versatility to provide enhanced and versatile data storage properties, including organized hierarchical data and efficient data updates with flexibility. Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications such as managing flood risks. While the shallow water equations are commonly employed for this purpose, their traditional numerical solutions can be time-consuming and require precise riverbed measurements. In this research, a two-step process is proposed to tackle this issue. Firstly, the probability distribution of the riverbed profile is estimated from flow velocity measurements using geostatistical analysis, enabling the prediction of flow velocities without the need for direct riverbed measurements. In the second stage, machine learning algorithms are used to develop a swift solver for the shallow water equations, which can be informed by future direct riverbed measurements. This approach facilitates the incorporation of new bathymetry data into the predictions, even if the riverbed profile changes over time. We evaluate and compare three fast solver models – PCA-DNN, SE, and SVE – and demonstrate that they can accurately predict flow velocities at a significantly lower computational cost compared to traditional methods, while validating our results on the Savannah River. This research provides a preliminary step towards developing a learning-based model that can adapt to changing riverbed profiles, and further optimization is needed to improve the performance of the solver. Nevertheless, our findings also demonstrate that even a basic DNN model can predict flow velocities at a considerably lower cost than traditional methods on a larger dataset, such as the Amazon River. This work paves the way for investigating more complex models and larger datasets in future research. The proposed methodology is applicable to the prediction of flow velocities in rivers, estuaries, and coastal oceans, and our results suggest that machine learning-based fast solvers can be an efficient tool for this purpose. This note provides an introduction to the interplay between Hodge-theoretic and geometric approaches to compactifying moduli spaces of algebraic varieties. We discuss algebraic compactifications, focusing on properties such as properness and compactness, and review the relationship between geometric and arithmetic compactifications. We also examine boundary behavior, via the valuation theory of algebraic geometry, and discuss the connection between Hodge numbers and geometric properties of compactified moduli spaces. We then outline various strategies for studying the compactness of general algebraic moduli spaces and provide a concise review of the relationship between compactifications and birational geometry. We conclude by examining specific results related to the compactness of moduli spaces of curves and surfaces and presenting an overview of the key issues related to higher-dimensional cases. We anticipate that this note will serve as a starting point for further exploration of the intricate connections between Hodge theory, algebraic geometry, and number theory.

Determining whether bulge growth causes the flattening of the star formation main sequence at the high mass end remains uncertain. To explore the role of bulges in forming the main sequence, a study examined the NUV$-r$ color of 6401 local star-forming galaxies by comparing the central and outer regions of each galaxy. Since NUV$-r$ color serves as a specific indicator of star formation rate, a distinction emerged when analyzing galaxies based on their stellar masses. At stellar masses less than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, there is only a small color difference between the central and outer NUV$-r$. Above this threshold, however, a more significant difference in color becomes apparent, indicating the central bulge in massive galaxies is more mature. Observing the behavior of galaxies based on their S\'ersic index $n$ also provided valuable insights. Those with an index of 2.0 or greater are more likely to exhibit redder NUV$-r$ colors even when considering factors like bulge-to-total mass ratio and stellar mass. This indicates a stronger relationship between star formation within bulges and $n$ (or central mass density) than with the B/T ratio. Notably, a sharp increase in galaxies with an index of 2.0 or greater occurs at stellar masses greater than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$. This pattern is consistent with the downturn observed in the mass-star formation rate relation at the same mass transition point. Therefore, it appears the growing presence of dense bulges with low specific star formation rates in massive galaxies is the key factor contributing to the flattened slope of the mass-star formation rate relation at the high mass end. This is supported by alternative explanations such as gas accretion rate limits or a constant gas fraction also showing a sharp transition point at the same mass level. The intrinsic spread in the mass-star formation rate relation remains limited to a factor of fifteen, regardless of whether the reference frame is based on the total stellar mass or the bulge mass alone. X-ray images contain subtle characteristics with predictive information about patients who are likely to experience severe COVID-19 symptoms.  If accurate, this hypothesis offers significant practical value in directing limited medical resources towards high-risk patients by leveraging an economical imaging method. However, confirming this hypothesis proves challenging due to the need for large, well-annotated data sets containing post-imaging severity outcome information. To address this issue, a novel approach is proposed for extracting crucial features from datasets with ICU admission labels, using interpretable models that integrate neural networks trained to identify lung abnormalities. By limiting model complexity, overfitting is minimized while maintaining the ability to interpret results. Interestingly, only a small set of features accounts for most of the variability between patients with severe symptoms. When applied to an unrelated, larger dataset comprising clinical notes related to lung pathologies, this approach is shown to accurately identify key image characteristics associated with specific locations within the lungs. Additionally, the proposed method highlights the statistical importance of previously unquantifiable features related to ICU admission, which was not explicitly captured before. Furthermore, notable aspects of the proposed method include its robustness in handling limited datasets, along with the incorporation of cutting-edge lung segmentation technology and the use of low-complexity models to prevent overfitting. To facilitate replication and advancement of the proposed approach, the code and methodology for the experiments are made publicly available. This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of false positives in VRD tasks. To counter the imbalance, SABRA incorporates Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), which divides proposals into distinct sub-classes based on difficulty and samples a balanced distribution accordingly. By employing this strategy, BNPS yields an optimized model performance and a notable decrease in false positives. To further address the challenging low-frequency proposals with spatial ambiguity, we refine the spatial modeling capability of SABRA in two ways: introducing a simple and efficient multi-head graph attention network to capture global object interactions and a spatial mask decoder that learns the local configuration. Our approach demonstrates superior performance compared to the current state-of-the-art methods across three datasets for human-object interaction and visual relationship detection. Code is available at GitHub: https://github.com/zwang96/SABRA.

We've performed an in-depth analysis of three galaxy cores at $\rm z=2.91$ within a massive galaxy group, yielding high-resolution infrared and submillimeter data. This revealed that the galaxies exhibit extremely compact, actively star-forming cores at the centers of massive, irregularly shaped disk systems, both of which exhibit quiescent, lopsided characteristics. Consequently, these galaxies are witnessing `outside-in' quenching. We propose a theoretical framework suggesting that mass asymmetry, resulting from absorbed and irregular matter, is accountable for their diminished star-formation activity by channeling it towards their core. Furthermore, we observe that disk asymmetry is associated with gas streams that are feeding the galaxies and influencing their evolution. This is manifested by an aligned major-axis of galaxies in relation to nearby filaments, presenting observational evidence of accretion streams on galaxy evolution. This is demonstrated by bulge construction, combined with massive quiescent, lopsided galaxies in the current stage, until they collide with a major merger galaxy. This collision will trigger rapid star formation in the developed bulge and eventually leads to the formation of massive, compact, quiescent galaxies similar to massive elliptical galaxies in the current stage. This can happen within a short period of $10^8$ years, primarily based on simulated interactions, combined with comprehensive, semi-analytical galaxy formation models that prove our findings, thus providing a deeper understanding of the complex, dynamic interactions between galaxies, combined with combined effects of their environment on their evolution. This is reflected in an unique visual representation consisting of multiple, interconnected streams of events that occurred in the past $\rm 10^9$ years, from the initial accretion of matter, combined with its distribution and streaming patterns, to the interaction with the surrounding environment, combined with the effects of massive star formation on galaxy evolution. This is further supported by multiple, individual detailed images of the individual galaxies, combined with their constituent parts, from the central massive star-forming regions, combined with the surrounding irregular disk systems, to the nearby filaments that are feeding them, combined with simulated interactions and combined effects of their evolution on the galaxy formation models. This research was primarily conducted using extensive, high-resolution near-infrared and submillimeter data obtained from the Hubble Space Telescope, combined with the Spitzer Space Telescope, the Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer, the Herschel Space Observatory, the Atacama Submillimeter Telescope, the Submillimetre Array, the IRAM 30-m Telescope

This study reveals intriguing evidence of a complex internal rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267654's rotation speed is observed to be higher near its surface rather than at its core, which presents a challenge to angular momentum conservation principles. To validate our findings, we updated the constraints based on spectroscopic surface measurements, verified that the detected oscillation patterns align with the previously determined core and outer layer rotation rates, and confirmed that the star exhibits no significant chemical abnormalities. Additionally, we eliminated the possibility of any interaction with a companion star that might be causing tidal forces. Lastly, we examined possible explanations for this unusual internal rotation profile, including the possibility of the star ingesting a giant planet or experiencing enhanced angular momentum redistribution through tidal inertial waves induced by a nearby substellar companion, and encouraged future observational and theoretical studies. Although primarily observational in nature, this study also includes theoretical predictions regarding the effects of a giant planet's ingestion on a star's internal rotation patterns. If true, these predictions could be tested through future direct detection of the lost planetary mass or detailed analysis of the stellar tidal inertial waves. Ultimately, this research highlights the complexities of angular momentum redistribution and conservation within low-mass giant stars and suggests that their internal rotation patterns cannot be fully understood without considering various factors, including possible planetary interactions, and provides a specific case study that can be compared to future theoretical predictions of unfathomably detailed asteroseismology on similar stars. This study was based on data obtained from the Kepler spacecraft and used a range of observational and analytical techniques to derive the initial and final rotation rates, confirmed the conservation of angular momentum, determined the core and outer layer rotation rates, defined the surface convection zone's extent, determined the star's chemical composition, ruled out external interactions with a companion star, and examined possible explanations for the complex internal rotation pattern. This research was conducted by combining public time series data from the Kepler spacecraft, high-resolution spectroscopic measurements from the Hobby-Eberly Telescope, and various analytical techniques including calculations of the rotation rates, analysis of oscillation patterns, determination of the surface convection zone's extent, assessment of the chemical composition, and investigation of possible interactions with a companion star. This study provides an individual case study of a low-mass giant

Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms due to its rapid dissemination and potential to cause harm worldwide. Although machine learning models have been successful in detecting false information, especially when large amounts of labeled data are available, their effectiveness significantly declines when they are applied to emerging events. This limitation creates a significant obstacle for the current methods in detecting false news on unexpected events. Furthermore, the fact that newly emerging events necessitate building a new model from scratch or retraining the existing one, which is often expensive, time-consuming and impractical in real-world settings. To address this challenge, an end-to-end fake news detection system called MetaFEND has been proposed, allowing for the rapid learning to identify false information on unexpected events with limited information from verified sources. This system leverages the strength of both meta-learning and neural process methods, incorporates a module to address label embedding, and employs a hard attention mechanism to enhance the effectiveness by dealing with category information and eliminating unnecessary information. Experiments conducted on large multimedia datasets obtained from Twitter and Weibo demonstrate the effectiveness of the MetaFEND system in detecting false information on previously unseen events and outperforms the current state-of-the-art techniques. Moreover, the system's ability to handle category information and eliminate unnecessary information was validated through a additional experiment. The source code of the MetaFEND system has been made available at https://github.com/ghaithan/MetaFEND. This system has vast potential applications in detecting false information on various social media platforms due to its versatility. This research paper examines a one-dimensional periodic transport equation featuring non-local flow and fractional decay. The equation in question is given by $$
u_{t}-(Hu)_{x}u_{x}+\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u=0,\quad (t,x)\in R^{+}\times S.
$$
Where $S$ denotes the domain, we have $\kappa\geq0$, $0<\alpha\leq1$, and investigate the well-posedness of this transport equation within $H^{3}(S)$ for a limited period of time. It is demonstrated that when $\kappa$ equals zero and the initial data is smooth and odd, the solution will eventually become singular over a finite period of time. Additionally, we find that introducing a weak dissipation term $\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u$ also leads to the formation of singularity in a finite amount of time. This research also provides bounds on the solution and the time it takes for the solution to become singular. Furthermore, for $u_{0}\in H^{3}(S)$ and given mild conditions on the initial data, we establish that the solution will become singular over a finite period of time $T_{\text{sing}}\in (0, C\|u_{0}\|_{H^{3}(S)}^{-1})$. Lastly, we compare this transport equation with the third derivative of the Navier--Stokes equations, where both models develop singularities in a finite amount of time when formulated in a periodic domain. This research was previously demonstrated in a non-periodic setting in [J. D. Wright, Invent. Math. 197, no. 3 (2014) pp. 443-504; J. D. Wright, Arch. Ration. Mech. Anal. 216, no. 2 (2015) pp. 449-501], and the development of the singularity is linked to the instability of the solution $u=\lambda^{-1}(\Lambda^{2}u_{0})$ under smooth and odd initial conditions. Finally, we formulate an open problem related to the dynamics of the solution $u=\lambda^{-1}(\Lambda^{2}u_{0})$ where $0<\lambda\leq 1$.

Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained popularity due to their utility in omnidirectional precoding techniques. This research extends Golay complementary matrices to higher-dimensional spaces known as multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays and presents novel construction methods for pairs and quadruples of GCA. A set of ring identities is introduced to facilitate these constructions. Specifically, it is shown that GCA pairs are possible in four-dimensional space if certain conditions are met concerning the sizes and their factorization. Additionally, in binary GCM quadruples, possible sizes are postulated as unlimited, which is confirmed for sizes 78x78 and a few scattered instances, whereas all positive integers below 1000 can be covered in a one-dimensional space of a quaternary GCM quad. Finally, a general framework for constructing GCM quadruples in any number of dimensions is presented. Perhaps of greater interest, a special class of idempotent matrices is defined that can be constructed using the ring method, and these matrices have properties analogous to those of the well-known Paley construction, offering promise for further insights. Quantum tunneling is an inherent process that lacks a direct analogy in classical physics, and it can rival Coulomb interactions to give rise to intricate phenomena.
In silicon, precise placement of phosphorus dopants is feasible to address the diverse consequences of this interplay, however this approach depends on wave functions related to crystal symmetry, which quantum tunneling inherently affects.
In this study, lattice-aperiodic valley interference patterns were directly visualized in silicon by employing scanning tunneling microscopy to investigate coupled atoms.
The examination reveals the significance of envelope anisotropy, valley interference and the location of the dopants on Heisenberg's spin exchange interaction in silicon.
The findings indicate that exchange interaction becomes immune to valley interference by arranging in-plane dopants in particular directions aligned with the crystallographic orientation, ultimately retrieving vacuum-like characteristics where the exchange interaction maximizes the overlap between donor orbitals, and the variation in pairs is minimized to less than 10-fold.
This robust exchange interaction remains over a considerable distance range, from a high-fidelity quantum computation regime influenced by Coulomb interaction to coupled donor arrays used in quantum simulations in silicon.

Complex systems consisting of multiple interacting components typically adhere to straightforward and universal principles, which underpin their intricate behaviors. Despite graph neural networks offering valuable insights for modeling these complex interactions, there's still a significant gap in understanding how to effectively generalize to novel instances of the same system type. In our investigation, we successfully applied graph neural networks to analyze a representative example of a nonlinear dynamical system – the belief propagation algorithm. By interpreting the learned representations and network components, we revealed their alignment with fundamental properties of the underlying probabilistic inference algorithm. Furthermore, we established a key relationship between the network's statistical interactions and its parameter configuration, which we termed the 'graph translator'. Leveraging this translator enabled us to explore two novel generalization capabilities. Firstly, we could extract the underlying structure of an unexplored system from observational time series data, without needing explicit access to the system itself. Secondly, we could generate a corresponding network from this recovered structure, paving the way for a deeper understanding of the dynamics and underlying architecture of complex systems and demonstrating the practical applications of this insight for future generalization. Notably, our approach and results are supported by graphical illustrations, numerical experiments, and a real-world example involving a nonlinear non-linear hidden Markov model. Our research finds its place within the community of machine learning at large, and more specifically within the graph neural network, complex system, and transfer learning frameworks. Our findings serve as a tangible example of how machine learning models can successfully distill the underlying physics from complex systems, and our code is available at https://github.com/ghul0u/BNP-explained.

These formulas have a meaningful interpretation within the framework of graded polynomial rings and enable us to derive computations related to homology modules in the context of stable homotopy theory, utilizing the properties of the mod $2$ Steenrod algebra. Additionally, we provide a novel formulation of a result by M. Moore (UNPUBLISHED) and offer an alternative proof of his finding. Our methods also enable us to determine the degrees of specific polynomial components, making this approach potentially useful for a broader range of problems related to the mod $2$ Steenrod algebra. Moreover, we establish connections between these counts and the concept of partial derivatives, offering an alternative perspective on a result by G. Hatert. Lastly, our work concludes by examining a particular instance in which the underlying ring is altered from the ring of integers, specifically the case of polynomial rings based on Gaussian integers, which leads to a new analytical framework incorporating the concept of complex variables and the application of the Cauchy residue theorem. This extended approach enables us to enumerate the counts of integer partitions for a broader range of scenarios, although it requires additional computational time. Evaluating the effectiveness of this treatment requires analyzing changes to the treated brain area after LITT, which can be achieved by accurately defining the treated region through image processing. Although deep learning techniques offer high precision in defining this region, training them requires a large amount of data which can be hard to obtain for a new and emerging treatment such as LITT. In response, this paper proposes an innovative framework called Progressive Brain Lesion Synthesis, consisting of multiple stages to artificially create more training data with various characteristics, thereby enhancing the precision of the therapy evaluation. Furthermore, the paper includes a design for encoding external information that can aid in training and improving segmentation results by integrating a condition and mask embedding block, resulting in better outcomes when compared to common image processing methods, according to experimental data. The proposed approach can be applied to other medical treatments beyond LITT. The code for this paper is available online at https://github.com/liyousef/Brain_Lesion_Synthesis. GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for efficient program analysis and verification, leveraging graph transformation rules to ease these tasks. However, efficiently developing GP 2 programs poses difficulties, primarily stemming from the time-consuming nature of graph matching. To overcome this limitation, the GP 2 framework incorporates a type of rooted rule that can be matched rapidly, given certain conditions are met. In order to accelerate the GP 2 compiler, several key modifications have been made to Bak's compiler, including a data structure optimisation for dynamic arrays known as BigArray. This novel structure, characterised by successive size increments of its components, enhances compiler performance. As evidence of the compiler's speed-enhancing benefits, a case study is presented showcasing the GP 2 compiler's application in optimising the runtime efficiency of a program aimed at detecting binary DAGs. This previously time-consuming operation is now executed at a linear rate following the compiler upgrade. Furthermore, the upgraded GP 2 compiler features BigArray data structures, a useful contribution to the Java programming community. Finally, the GP 2 environment is demonstrated to be particularly effective in tackling large-scale program analysis tasks. In support of these findings, complete implementation details of the GP 2 compiler and the previously mentioned program are provided. Additionally, a previously published paper by Serani et al. is built upon, with a previously overlooked issue in their program's implementation identified and resolved. As a result, a more reliable and more efficient solution is now available, capable of efficiently verifying certain aspects of Java binary files. This new solution, known as the Javalist verifier, is presented alongside the GP 2 compiler case study. In response to the challenges posed by dynamic memory allocation, the GP 2 compiler has also been further enhanced with the addition of a static array optimisation known as StaticBigArray. This new version of the GP 2 compiler is available for download, along with the Javalist verifier and the binary DAG detector, along with the GP 2 development kit. This kit provides a comprehensive environment for developing GP 2 programs, featuring an integrated development interface, a runtime system, and a range of pre-written GP 2 libraries. In conclusion, the GP 2 compiler has been successfully improved, with a resulting verifer, known as Javalist2, found to be not only more efficient but also more reliable, with a further version, known as Javalist2Fast, developed to enhance performance further, with both of these solutions validated through the use of GP 2 to detect binary AspectJ

The framework's initial step constructs unique contrastive learning graphs to differentiate between similar and dissimilar data points, with a focus on optimizing a contrastive loss function to obtain the projection matrix. The framework's capability to handle similar and dissimilar data enables the integration of unsupervised and supervised feature extraction techniques. We further developed three specific methods: an unsupervised contrastive learning technique and two supervised contrastive learning approaches. Our framework's superiority is demonstrated through comprehensive numerical experiments conducted on five real-world datasets, resulting in performance improvements over existing methods. The framework's potential for optimizing contrastive learning for feature extraction beyond the listed methods is also shown. Our findings expand upon a framework initially proposed by Giudici, Li, and Praeger by providing an infinite number of examples classified under the star normal quotient twisted wreath category for locally arc-transitive graphs. A particular focus is given on the infinite sequence of 2-arc-transitive graphs included within this category. Our study also implies the existence of an infinite number of locally arc-transitive 2-arc-transitive graphs classified under the twisted wreath category for a finite group action. Furthermore, we establish a finite group $G$ is uniquely determined as the group executing a twisted wreath action on $\mathbb{Z}_p^d$, and this action is realized by a specific infinite sequence of group extensions, ultimately leading to a graph theory interpretation of this action. A notable finding within our research reveals that the regular representation of the symmetric group $S_{p^d}$ contains a composition series defined by the action of a twisted wreath group on the set $\mathbb{Z}_{p^d}$. Ultimately, our work on the twisted wreath framework enables us to determine the structure of a particular group $G$ executed over the set $\mathbb{Z}_p^d$, from a group theory perspective. A related problem also is addressed in our research, specifically the question of identifying the group executed over the set $\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$. A special case related to the Aronszajn sequence is provided in this instance. A significant observation related to the general twisted wreath framework, as well as a related star normal quotient property, is then determined for the set $\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$ executed by a certain group $G$. Working with categorical data for model selection and sparse modeling becomes increasingly complex as the number of variables grows, as it typically requires a parameter for each category, making interpretation challenging. Despite its efficiency for handling continuous and categorical variables, the Group Lasso often results in inconsistent estimates, rendering the model difficult to interpret due to the lack of sparsity. To achieve a sparse solution using the Group Lasso, we propose a two-step method: first reducing data dimensions through the Group Lasso, and then employing an information criterion on a subset of clustered models. This algorithm's performance is evaluated under high-dimensional conditions and compared with state-of-the-art methods using synthetic and real-world datasets, showing its superior performance in terms of prediction accuracy and model size. In particular, this paper shows that the proposed method can lead to a sparse solution using the Group Lasso, and provides theoretical guarantees for its performance in high-dimensional conditions. In addition, this paper provides a new interpretation of the Group Lasso estimate for binary categorical data, showing that it is effective in selecting important categories. In line with standard practice, all simulations were conducted under a working knowledge assumption, where the number of clusters and the number of categories are known in advance. In this case, the proposed method can be implemented by selecting the number of clusters and the number of categories through the information criterion used in the second step of the algorithm. In particular, the paper shows that under a working knowledge assumption, the Group Lasso estimate can be viewed as a weighted average of the parameter values across each category, allowing for inference to be made about the importance of each category. In addition, the paper provides a new perspective on the condition required to ensure consistency in the Group Lasso estimate, showing that the number of categories should be less than the square root of the sample size for the algorithm to perform optimally. Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous language tasks. However, the potential for these models to effectively utilize structured information, particularly within knowledge graphs, compared to free-form text, has not been extensively explored. To bridge this knowledge gap, our approach develops a method to incorporate structured knowledge into LLMs through training on specific knowledge graph triples. We demonstrate that LLMs pre-trained with our technique on a vast knowledge base like Wikidata outperform conventional T5 models in various evaluation benchmarks. Specifically, our approach shows comparable performance when compared to training models on descriptive language containing the same information, and significantly improves performance when utilizing smaller knowledge graphs. To improve modeling long sequences in the time domain for speech separation, a dual-path RNN was previously proposed by dividing lengthy sequences into shorter chunks and processing them with internal and external RNN components. Building upon this work, a Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN) model is presented here by integrating the dual-path RNN with Convolution Recurrent Networks. The model's RNN components were substituted with dual-path modules where internal components were used to analyze single-frame spectral patterns, and external components were used to analyze consecutive frame dependencies. Notably, with only 0.8 million parameters, the DPCRN model achieved an overall mean opinion score (MOS) of 3.57 in the wideband scenario of the Interspeech 2021 DNS challenge. Evaluations across additional datasets have shown the efficacy of this model. The code for the DPCRN model is now publicly available at github.com/lingyu-93/DPCRN.

Reconstructing a quantum state of continuous-variable systems like the radiation field is complicated, mainly due to the high dimensionality of its Hilbert space. Multiple approaches have been proposed for state reconstruction, including conventional methods and machine learning applications, yet there's no universally effective protocol for deriving the Wigner function from an optical tomogram of an arbitrary light state. We demonstrate that specific non-classical effects such as the generation of entanglement and onset of quantum synchronization are directly reflected in distinct patterns of optical tomograms, eliminating the need for full state reconstruction in these instances. Specifically, we show that the generation of entanglement between two independent oscillators or the onset of synchronization between two coupled oscillators leaves a distinctive signature on their joint optical tomograms. By inspecting these patterns, one can gain insight into the level of quantum correlation and synchronization between systems, thereby offering a more efficient approach to state reconstruction in such situations. The proposed strategy is particularly applicable to small-dimensional systems where the dimensionality of the Hilbert space is comparable to the number of optical tomogram bins. The reflectometry-based quantum state reconstruction, a physical implementation of this method, has already been achieved for a low-dimensional system similar to a qutrit. The reflectometry technique involves measuring the intensity of light scattered off a state-dependent optical element, which is directly related to the pattern of the optical tomogram, and provides a practical means of detecting the generation of entanglement or the onset of synchronization between systems. The proposed approach offers a balanced solution for the trade-off between the accuracy of state reconstruction and the difficulty of implementing the procedure, and has potential applications in the analysis of complex systems such as open quantum systems, discrete optical automata, and open discrete time-coherent systems. The reflectometry-based approach can also be used to investigate unique properties of continuous-variable systems including non-reciprocity, where the flow of quantum information moves in one direction, and where the generation of entanglement or the onset of synchronization is affected by the presence of non-reciprocity. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its class and the network's decision boundaries, which is used to assign a soft label to the sample. This allows for the model to be trained via standard knowledge distillation methods. When access to the original data isn't possible, pseudo-samples are created based on the network's decision boundaries and assigned soft labels, which serve as a transfer set for training the model. Our proposed approach is evaluated on multiple networks and datasets and shows positive results. Code is available at: https://github.com/zwang84/zsdb3kd.

Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Experimentation across multiple scenarios highlights the superiority of our Co-Imitation Learning framework, confirming the benefits of inter-agent knowledge exchange in the absence of external supervision. Using reinforcement learning post maximum likelihood estimation pre-training can significantly improve neural machine translation efficiency. Nonetheless, a notable issue with RL for NMT arises from the large action space hindering its performance, as our hypothesis proposes. We've conducted two series of experiments which support this assumption and yield notable outcomes. Firstly, reducing the vocabulary's size enhances the RL's effectiveness, as our findings indicate. Furthermore, a notable improvement can be observed when the action space is reduced without changing the vocabulary, as validated by multiple metrics including BLEU scores, semantic similarity and human assessment. Our research discovered that initializing the final fully connected layer with a layer that generalizes action similarities resulted in substantial RL performance gains, averaging 1.5 BLEU points improvement. We believe these findings are relevant to a wide range of RL applications involving large action spaces. The code is available at github.com/AlexKiselyov/RL-NMT-big-action-space-learning.

dynamics in the laboratory using a single photon system that is linked to its surroundings.
Our theory encompasses all experimental observations and provides an in-depth
analysis of the system's non-equilibrium steady state.

environment can be precisely managed to ensure that there is continuous, two-way 
flow of information between the open system and the surrounding environment. Our

system can reach, all of which are controlled by a single parameter.

discrete time-driven dynamics.

A rational number p/q represents the basis for a numbering system. Words composed of digits 0 through p-1 in base p/q correspond to unique rational numbers, which make up the set Np/q. While previous studies on base p/q systems focus on evaluating words that translate to nonnegative integers, our analysis examines subsets of (Np/q)d that are identifiable using finite automata in (Ap)d. Our initial contribution identifies the subsets defined by first-order logic similar to those defined by the Bachi-Bruyere Theorem in integer base systems. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that both natural order relation and modulo-q operator are not recognisable within base p/q systems. Additionally, our results classify the operator modulo p as recognizable, presenting a distinct case where the operator modulo q is recognizable if and only if p is divisible by q. Our study also examines the structure of machine recognisable languages in base p/q systems and identifies them as being composed of a stack-based pushdown automaton and a finite state automaton, along with a rule-based generator that utilises the division and remainder operations to generate the next state from a state and the current input. Our findings further demonstrate that the pushdown stack can be restricted to a single layer consisting of the quotient state at the top, which allows us to determine the quotient state q' from the current quotient state q, the input digit d, and the transition function that combines these elements. Our approach also enables us to determine the set of all possible quotient states that are recognisable, which, after converting to a equivalent form, can be found to be equal to the set {0, p/q, 2p/q,..., (p-1)p/q}. Our study finally examines the relationship between base p/q systems and base p systems, which involves converting words in base p/q to base p systems by introducing a new symbol representing the unknown part of the rational number and a set of rewrite rules that, along with the standard base p rules, determines the sequence of output digits. Our findings demonstrate that the recognition of a language in base p systems is equivalent to the recognition of the same language in base p/q systems, and vice versa. Our study also examines the difference between these two systems, which results in the recognition of a language in base p/q systems being capable of including the information about the exponent of the q component in the rational number, which, as mentioned earlier, is undecidable. Our findings provide a new perspective on the relationship between base p/q and base p systems

MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, distributed NoSQL database that allows for three different types of transactions: standalone, replica set, and sharded cluster deployments. Considering the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB transactions in each deployment, we investigated their transactional protocols. However, we found that the documentation for these protocols is unclear, particularly in regards to pseudocode and formal specifications of the consistency guarantees they provide. In our work, we clarified the transactional protocols for each MongoDB deployment, using pseudocode derived from official documentation and source code, and verified that they conform to specific variants of snapshot isolation. Our approach also enables efficient checking of the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB's transaction protocols. We contributed these findings to the CoSP website. Moreover, we developed a tool that can be used to extend this kind of analysis to other database protocols. We tested this tool on MongoDB's protocol and found that it provides a more concise and clear specification of the transactional consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB. Our research was conducted during an internship at the French National Center for Scientific Research (CNRS), and we presented our results at the NORDIS workshop held as part of the ECOOP conference. Our code and contributions to CoSP are available under the Apache-2 license. Our tool can be used to extend this kind of analysis to other database protocols. Research on intricate systems from the human brain to social connections has uncovered a higher-level structure that can be characterized through aggregates of interconnected triangles. To uncover these concealed geometric patterns, researchers are using topological methods and advanced graph theory to analyze and study dynamic processes occurring within these complex networks. This study leverages a recently developed model for triangle-based network assembly, where nanoscale triangular structures undergo spin reversal due to magnetic forces between connected nodes, fostering geometric frustration that drives novel phenomena in condensed matter physics. By manipulating the model's parameters, researchers observe how the shift from pair-based to triangular interactions affects ordering patterns, influencing the shape of resulting hysteresis loops. Moreover, the associated noise exhibited robust indicators of self-organization criticality, an emergent property solely induced by the intricate geometry of the network and not any inherent disorder. Consequently, this study demonstrates the practical utility of modeling networks as composed of interacting triangles, paving the way for further investigations into hidden geometric dynamics across diverse complex systems. Lastly, this research highlights the exceptional suitability of spin reversal in nanoassemblies as a realistic model for in-depth study, coupled with its direct applicability to various intricate networks beyond nanoassemblies.

We studied the solar wind energy flux near the inner edge of our solar system using data from four different close approaches to the sun by the Parker Solar Probe, where we recorded data for 12-day periods right around each encounter. These observations took place as close as 27.8 times the radius of the sun from the solar center, and we based our energy flux calculations on readings for electron density, temperature, and speed, along with the bulk characteristics of solar protons. Combining the data from the four approaches, we found the average energy flux that could reach the solar surface and counteract gravity is about 70 Watts per square meter, plus or minus 14 Watts. Notably, this is similar to the findings of other researchers using data from different spacecraft and covering a longer time period, but with a key difference being that the solar wind energy distributions were much more symmetrical and normally distributed than seen closer to the Earth, likely due to the influence of solar plasma fluctuations being limited by the close distance. Furthermore, the underlying solar wind patterns remained consistent between each of the four periods, allowing us to combine the data and better understand the overall variation in solar wind patterns, especially the 11-year solar cycle change, which we estimate is around 20 percent over the relevant time period based on solar activity readings. However, more research is needed to confirm this trend and evaluate the impact of solar protons on this calculation. Lastly, the high sensitivity of these energy flux measurements to the accuracy of electron density readings highlights the need for more precise measurements of this variable in future solar observations.

The study of cosmic microwave background anisotropies is a fundamental tool in physical cosmology research. However, the signal's weakness necessitates sophisticated and highly sensitive experiments that observe the sky across various frequencies with thousands of polarisation-sensitive detectors. As such experiments become increasingly sensitive, they are susceptible to being limited by instrumental systematic effects when trying to fully utilise their data. This paper presents a Python tool,'s4cmb', which generates simulated raw data streams in the time domain for contemporary cosmic microwave background experiments based on bolometric technology. The package also incorporates realistic instrumental systematic effects into the simulated data, with the goal of helping researchers assess the impact of such effects on actual data, informing future instrument design, and making simulated data sets more realistic for the development of accurate data analysis techniques. The package is particularly suitable for large-scale simulations required by modern cosmic microwave background experiments. The tool is openly available at https://github.com/ricardolopez/s4cmb. The current version of's4cmb' focuses exclusively on experiments using bolometric detectors, but it provides a suitable framework for extending its capabilities to different detector technologies. The code includes examples of simple simulations, background construction, and systematic effect addition, in addition to more complex scenarios involving multi-detector arrays and systematic effects changing over time. The tool can be used through a command line interface or interactively with a Python shell. The package includes functionalities for generating simulated streams from theoretical cosmic microwave background signals, as well as instrumental systematic effects based on real experiments, with the goal of conducting actual data analyses. The code is highly customisable, with features for incorporating user-defined systematic effects and detectors, the ability to save and load simulated streams and detectors, and the facility to plot simulated data streams and systematic effects. The package also includes tutorials and examples available on its website. The tool is an open source resource for the scientific community, with applications in experimental design, forward modelling, and data analysis development. In the task of arranging unordered words into a meaningful order, prior approaches rely on either linear models or neural networks, without examining the role of pre-trained language models, including why they would be beneficial. Utilizing BART as an example, we find it to be a suitable model for this task and explore its capabilities by conducting additional analysis using probing, which reveals that the syntactic dependencies inherent to BART significantly contribute to its performance. Furthermore, we discover improvements in using BART in a related task known as partial tree linearization. Our research highlights the importance of linguistic knowledge embedded within pre-trained language models and shows that at least in part, their performance can be attributed to this embedded knowledge, not solely cosine similarities. Our code has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghruvo/word-ordering. Our findings have been published in the proceedings of the Human Language Technology Conference 2022.

The rapid dissemination of ultra-realistic media over social platforms necessitates the immediate development of an efficient and adaptable technique for identifying deepfakes. Deepfake creation methods inadvertently leave distinguishing patterns in the frequency spectra of fabricated images and videos. Leveraging this insight, our research introduces a novel detection method, known as the MD-CSDNetwork, which combines features from spatial and frequency domains to derive a unified, discriminative representation for deepfake classification. The proposed network architecture, comprising two parallel branches processing spatial and frequency information, is designed to treat multiple domain inputs as interconnected learning signals. Through cross-stitch connections between the branches, our system automatically identifies an optimal blend of domain-specific and shared features, thereby enhancing performance and generalization. Evaluations conducted on the widely-used FaceForeniscs++ benchmark demonstrate improved classification results for various manipulation types and comparable performance to state-of-the-art approaches on the Celeb-DF and Deepfake Detection Dataset. Our system's versatility allows easy integration into popular deepfake detection datasets, yielding results that outperform current benchmarks. Our code has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghru/MD-CSDNetwork.

In 1930, mathematician K. Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized for use in metric and semi-metric spaces. Building upon this foundation, he presented two specific problems concerning the embedding of spaces with angle functions into the structure of Euclidean spaces. Over time, researchers focused on these problems, though only in the context of certain specific types of metric spaces. This article aims to enhance the definition of angle function to accommodate spaces with the property of betweenness, which it deems a more fundamental framework. Within this revised framework, the article provides solutions to Menger's initially posed problems. Furthermore, the article also offers an answer to at least one part of a second problem previously unresolved by the author. Additionally, it includes an appendix containing an independent result of some interest. Lastly, the article discusses Menger's M-space concept and demonstrates that it is equivalent to a specific variant of the betweenness spaces defined using angle functions, albeit with an important condition regarding the characterizations of points, which proves to be a challenging aspect. This condition is not met by certain popularly used data structures, thereby providing a novel interpretation of the famous data processing problem known as the point problem. The article's results can be further extended to also address and solve two other previously unresolved problems. The article's methodology can be viewed as a combination of the methods advocated by P. Erdos during the 1963 conference held in Budapest, specifically the use of "elementary" proofs that involve as little mathematics as possible and the concentration on problems within the field of geometry. The article also includes a biographic note regarding the life and academic career of K. Menger. The article's results were originally published in the journal Mathematica Slovaca, volume 70, number 6, pages 1181-1200, and in the journal Archives of Mathematical Logic, volume 56, number 7, pages 663-674. The article further provides a solution to the problem of determining whether the angle function defined by the slope of lines can be considered continuous. This problem originally appeared in the book titled Mathematical Problems, published in 1967 by the Institute of Mathematics of the Polish Academy of Sciences, and also in the book titled Selected Problems of Mathematics, published in 1970, though neither of these books provided the answer to this problem. The article's results were previously presented at the conference titled Geometry and Topology of Manifolds, held in 2013 in Baia Gherghite

Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive examination of these schemes has been unfeasible until now. This research undertakes an empirical analysis of Forsage, a high-profile pyramid scheme built into a blockchain smart contract, with unprecedented visibility of its transactions. By utilizing Forsage's publicly accessible code and transaction records, our study explores the intricate workings of the scheme, its impact on users, and its evolution. Our data highlights the enormous financial gains enjoyed by the top participants as well as the significant losses suffered by nearly nine out of ten users. By reviewing the code manually and through the use of a custom-made transaction simulator, as well as examining promotional content on videos and social media, our findings reveal the deceptive strategies used by Forsage promoters to deceive users and the limited geographical reach of the scheme. Our data coverage spans from the launch of the scheme in April 2020 until the end of October 2021, a period during which the scheme distributed approximately $321 million in profits to its participants. Our study sheds light on the innovative ways Forsage promoters exploited linguistic ambiguities and cryptic blockchain transactions to operate below the radar of regulatory authorities, as well as the scheme's success in attracting a particular demographic of users. Our analysis of Forsage provides a unique insight into pyramid scams and other similar decentralized investment scams. Our research also highlights the difficulties that users face when trying to understand the inner workings of these schemes, as well as the challenges of effectively regulating them. Our findings suggest that these schemes are incredibly resilient and can thrive in environments with minimal legal oversight. Our data and research tools, which include the code and a transaction simulator, are available for further study and analysis. Our research into Forsage also has implications for the broader context of the blockchain industry and provides valuable insights that can be applied to a various range of decentralized applications, including pyramidal scams like Forsage, which are designed to manipulate the ordering of transactions in a way that exploits the characteristics of blockchains. Our study into Forsage has been conducted in a way that minimizes judgment and focuses instead on presenting objective facts about the scheme and its operations, as well as providing context for the environment in which it existed. Our research into Forsage provides a unique opportunity for further analysis and interpretation by experts in the fields of economics, computer science, and law. The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters remains incomplete. We have investigated 19 newly proposed globular cluster candidates located in the galaxy's bulge using infrared color-magnitude diagrams and the VVV survey database. We calculated key astrophysical properties including the reduction of light passing through interstellar gas, distance from Earth, total brightness, average cluster movement through space, metal composition, and age. We constructed a catalog of likely cluster members using vector motion diagrams and removed extraneous stars from the observed data. We estimate a broad range of light obstruction and gas reduction across the sample clusters as expected within the galaxy's bulge. We calculated their distances from Earth as being between 6.8 to 11.4 kiloparsecs and consequently determined that the clusters could be anywhere between 0.56 to 3.25 kiloparsecs from the galaxy's center. We compared their motion to typical galaxy bulge movements except for VVV-CL160, whose movement was distinct. We calculated their metallic content and ages, discovering metal contents between minus one and four tenths and ages between 8 to 13 billion years. We calculated total brightness levels both in the infrared K-band and the visual V-band and found a range from minus 3.4 to minus 7.5 in visual brightness levels. We further analyzed the possible presence of RR Lyrae stars found within the proposed cluster regions, basing our findings on positions, motion, metal composition, and ages, and comparing the data with previous research, ultimately classifying nine candidates as confirmed globular clusters, seven others needed further investigation, and the remaining three as open clusters rather than globular ones. We also explored possible distances for five clusters that had previously defined distances, employing the RR Lyrae stars within those regions and calculated new distances ranging from 7.0 to 11.5 kiloparsecs, which in turn ranged from 0.26 to 3.4 kiloparsecs from the galaxy's center. We discovered nine recognized globular clusters, six new ones, and four possible ones, along with three that were actually open clusters. One of the newly proposed clusters, VVV-CL160, was notable due to its distinct movement, while another, E3-cl 207, had a composition and age similar to the galaxy's bulge and thus needed further investigation to confirm its status. Thousands of white-light stellar flares are now being observed through high precision, long-baseline photometry from space missions including Kepler, K2, and TESS, which provide vital information for assessing exoplanetary biosignatures and the habitability of planets in low-mass stars' UV environments. Despite this advancement, a critical limitation remains in assessing these variables, which stems from the lack of data on near-ultraviolet spectral stellar flares. As such, a grid of updated radiative-hydrodynamic simulations, which incorporates enhanced pressure broadening of hydrogen lines, is being used to predict the continuum flux of $\lambda \approx 1800-3300$ Å\  in a well-studied superflare from AD Leo during its peak phases. This prediction model utilizes semi-empirical combinations of radiative electron beam flux spectra consisting of two electron beam models: a high-flux simulation with a high energy cutoff and a lower-flux simulation with a lower energy cutoff. This two-component approach effectively explains the Balmer line broadening, the optical color temperature, the Balmer jump strength, and the far-ultraviolet continuum in the peak phases of this flare. Additionally, a comparative analysis is conducted with solar flare data, including those from the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph, which provide spatial resolution, combined with previous modeling of the SOL20140329T17:48 X1 solar flare, to demonstrate that the two-component electron beam model can be interpreted as the superposition of bright flare kernels and weaker ribbons in a larger area. This indicates that even mild ribbons in longer wavelengths can contain extreme far-ultraviolet radiative signatures in massive stellar flares, with enough power to photoionize a planetary upper atmosphere, with implications for exoplanetary biosignatures and the habitability of planets in low-mass stars' UV environments. This model can be a valuable tool for predicting the effects of large flares on planetary atmospheres and for assessing the validity of future exoplanetary biosignatures in the near-ultraviolet region. Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulations intended to mislead them with subtle alterations like rotation and stretching. To address this, our proposed framework called TPC delivers precise and efficient security guarantees for these models against deceptive transformation-based attacks. Initially, we classify frequent three-dimensional transformations into three types: shearable (such as stretching), compositional (such as rotating), and indirectly compositional (such as skewing) transformations, then we outline general robustness validation strategies for all categories. Additionally, we design unique validation protocols tailored to a variety of specific transformation scenarios. Experimental results on multiple frequent three-dimensional transformations demonstrate the exceptional performance of TPC surpassing current standards with notable improvements. As an example, our method achieves significant enhancement in validated accuracy when dealing with twisting transformation along the z-axis (within a 20-degree range) from 20.3% to 83.8%. All code and models are available for use at https://github.com/Qianhewu/Point-Cloud-Smoothing.

Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. Developing a neural text generation model using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains a difficult task because the training process is non-differentiable. Current training methods are plagued by unreliable gradient calculations and inaccurate sentence representations. To address this challenge, we draw upon the principle of sparse coding to create the SparseGAN model, which generates compact, semantically-rich sentence representations to input into the discriminator. By leveraging an over-complete dictionary of embedding matrices and combining them into a minimal set of selected word embeddings, we achieve representations that not only facilitate efficient adversarial training by reducing noise but also enable a fully differentiable training process. Experimental evaluations on various text generation datasets demonstrate improved performance, particularly in terms of sequence-level metrics like BLEU scores. Moreover, we discover that each dimension of the sparse code corresponds to a specific linguistic element, and by analyzing these codes, we can identify interesting patterns of linguistic composition. We have made SparseGAN available as an application for natural language processing researchers, providing a novel approach to efficient text generation and establishing a new standard for comparative studies of GAN-based text generation models. Another significant focus of wildlife research involves calculating population size and density.  New spatial capture-recapture models can achieve this goal using individual encounter histories combined with location information from captures.  These models incorporate encounter probability functions connected to resource selection functions. We present a statistical method that integrates capture data from various sources with telemetry data to model these components jointly and provides a likelihood-based estimation framework to estimate the SCR and RSF model parameters at once. Notably, our study reveals that capture-recapture models alone can infer parameters for resource selection functions, enabling the exclusive use of capture data to investigate space usage, albeit with lower precision.  Nonetheless, using telemetry data yields superior precision. The integration of formal verification and testing techniques aims to provide improvements in creating and testing dependable software, as well as its ongoing development. Our geometric testing theory is designed to be a blueprint for a testing environment that can be part of a toolchain used by software developers, including professionals and academics in computer science. This environment features a sophisticated automated tool that can identify mistakes found during testing and help fix them by visually presenting the underlying causes in a graphical format on a screen. This format can be easily navigated to pinpoint areas of the code that need adjustment to resolve the issue. The underlying principles of our testing theory are under development and we welcome feedback and suggestions from anyone with an interest in this topic. The geometric testing theory has been applied to a real-world project, an open-source email program, to demonstrate its capabilities and the effectiveness of this approach. The code for this program, along with the testing framework and tools, is available for public use under the Apache Open Source License. The website www.geometric-testing.org provides more information about this project. The experiences and lessons learned from developing this project have been presented in a series of papers that can be found on the same website. The geometric testing theory and related tools can be used for other projects, although some adjustments might be necessary in some cases. The development of a reliable automated tool that identifies the causes of errors requires a perfect understanding of the code being tested and as such is a milestone in itself. The achievement of this level of understanding by the tool can be compared to the level of understanding that an instructor has of a student taking a course, as it's the result of analyzing a vast number of activities undertaken by that student. The geometric testing theory has the potential to be a foundation for a wide range of applications in the field of computer science, including education. The development of reliable and compliant software, especially in areas that require significant complexity and scalability, often results in a never-ending battle against time and resources. The employment of full automatic verification methods is often impractical due to the extensive amount of time and computational power required, which in turn leads to the use of verification rules that were previously tested manually, a process that in itself is very time-consuming and demanding. The necessity for reliable software, coupled with the limitations mentioned above, highlights the importance of a efficient testing method that can be part of a toolchain used by developers. The absence of an efficient testing method leads to the delivery of incomplete software that requires continuous tweaking and patching, which in turn results in a level of instability for the end user
