We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically when the network contains a large number of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge, unbounded processing power, and the ability to manipulate the protocol freely. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse, complex network's size, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) - where delta can be any arbitrarily small positive constant. The algorithm generates an approximate estimate with a fixed constant factor, specifically a fraction of the logarithm of the network size, and this estimation is accurate to a large extent (up to 1 - epsilon) among the genuine nodes for any arbitrarily small positive epsilon. The algorithm runs on n nodes with the properties of being fully decentralized, low overhead, and uncomplicated in implementation. Furthermore, the algorithm executes within O(log^3(n)) rounds, necessitates nodes to transmit small data packets in each round, and entails a minimal computation expense per round for each node. The accuracy of the algorithm is proven through a probabilistic argument, and we also compare it to a rival estimation algorithm previously known to achieve a certain level of accuracy in a much more limited setting. The existing algorithm is 2-logarithmic, whereas our new algorithm is (1-delta)*log(n). The previous record for the number of malicious nodes that the algorithm could handle was O(n beta) for any positive constant beta, and we surpass that by setting beta equal to 1. Finally, our result also implies the feasibility of a wide range of decentralized network tasks that require knowledge of the network size, such as a reliable consensus protocol, a leader election, a lottery, a clock synchronization protocol, and a random number generator, all of which can be achieved in a network of this type even with a large number of malicious nodes. The challenge of implementing these tasks in a decentralized manner is significantly reduced, and we achieve this by combining a particular estimation algorithm that is both accurate and efficient, as well as new lottery-based techniques that are robust in the presence of uncertainty. The development of this algorithm involves a complex probabilistic analysis of a complex, complex random variable known as the size of the giant component in an Erdős-Rényi random graph, and this analysis is a novel aspect of our research. The result is a new, rigorous probability theory theorem with implications that extend far beyond the scope of network size estimation. In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering field configurations from rescaled quantities is inherently challenging. Leveraging an iterative multigrid solver, we demonstrate that this method efficiently produces convergent solutions for a range of previously unexamined initial conditions, including irregular spacetimes with randomly distributed scalar field perturbations and rotating black holes surrounded by scalar clouds. The development of an advanced solver in conjunction with this approach enables the creation of high-quality initial data that meet precise simulation requirements, as shown in a study involving the collapse of scalar boson stars. Our code, named CTTK, is an open-source modification of the Singularity SPH code and supports both Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition and the novel algebraic choice, allowing for direct comparison of different initialization conditions. Recent discoveries of an anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have revitalized the study and manipulation of this phenomenon. A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. However, information about the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials is scarce due in part to the experimental challenge of measuring the anomalous Nernst coefficient accurately. Our study presents an investigation of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN thin films, facilitated by a simultaneous measurement of the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects using the same sample and experimental setup, allowing a direct comparison and precise quantification of the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity. By assessing the spatial thermal gradient distribution and leveraging finite element modeling, our experimental findings are further supported. We find that the anomalous Nernst coefficient in Mn$_3$NiN exhibits a small value of approximately 1.1$\times 10^{-5}$ cm$^2$/K, and our results also highlight the potential of this material to exhibit very little drift in measurement, likely due to its unique zero-magnetization property. Our study demonstrates a novel approach to measuring the anomalous Nernst effect and explores the promising magnetic and thermal transport properties of Mn$_3$NiN, offering potential applications in thermal to electrical energy conversion.

Understanding and identifying functional materials rely heavily on imaging, scattering, and spectroscopy. Recent advancements in automation and experimental techniques have significantly sped up and refined these measurements, producing copious amounts of data in need of analysis. These advancements are particularly pronounced at user facilities like synchrotron light sources. To process and interpret large datasets quickly, machine learning methods are continually being developed for real-time use in conjunction with measurements. Despite these developments, users without machine learning expertise often face significant barriers to integrating this technology into their experiments. To overcome these obstacles, this work presents several examples of machine learning models designed for real-time analysis across multiple beamlines at the National Synchrotron Light Source II (NSLS-II), with a focus on incorporating them into existing workflows to enable easy integration into experiments. By leveraging this framework, users can easily combine machine learning models with their existing workflows via the Bluesky Suite for data management and experimental orchestration. We demonstrate this approach across scattering and spectroscopic measurements, including a resonant scattering experiment, and analyze a dataset from a scanning imaging experiment. The framework and models presented are accessible through the Bluesky Repository, an open-platform for sharing and managing research components. To facilitate further development and customization, the repository provides accessible code, along with documentation on the beamline setup and data reduction techniques used. The approach and framework introduced here serve as a foundation for developing and deploying machine learning applications at user facilities, with the goal of enabling widespread access to this technology for users without machine learning expertise. The framework has been successfully utilized on multiple beamlines at the NSLS-II, with applications in physics, chemistry, biology, and environmental sciences. We establish a precise result for optimal solutions in an isoperimetric problem outside a confined object within the scenario where a large amount of space is considered, denoted as the 'large volume regime.' This achievement comes from a deeper examination of a specific surface-related problem that includes an unknown boundary, both within the confined object and at an infinitely distant point. The analysis involves the discovery of a specific term in an equation, termed 'isoperimetric residue,' which helps in expanding an isoperimetric problem equation when the 'large volume regime' is approached. Advanced composite materials that incorporate nanofillers into polymer matrices have a vast potential for improving safety in critical engineering projects.
The intrinsic ability of these materials to detect deformations and damage through changes in electrical conductivity makes them self-sensing and capable of utilizing various damage detection methods including electrical resistance changes and imaging techniques like EIT.
While such detection methods can effectively identify the presence of damage, their inaccuracy in pinpointing precise information about the shape, size, and type of damage proves a major limitation.
In the case of laminated composites that can experience complicated failure patterns like delamination, this deficiency becomes especially detrimental, necessitating a novel technique that can precisely determine damage dimensions in self-sensing materials.
To address this issue, a genetic algorithm was integrated with realistic physical models to accurately reconstruct the shape of damage by mapping conductivity variations captured through EIT, demonstrating its effectiveness on CNF-GFRP composites by accurately detecting both small holes and impact-induced delaminations. 
The successful results illustrate the capability of coupling piezoresistive properties with imaging and physics-based analysis to enhance the capacity of self-sensing composite materials to accurately determine damage configurations. 
The proposed method can be applied to a wide range of projects that utilize composite materials, from aerospace to sports equipment. 
Furthermore, by utilizing conductivity rather than resistance, a novel conductivity-based EIT reconstruction technique was developed, offering a better understanding of composite material conductivity and facilitating real-world applications. 
The development of this technique and the proposed algorithm can also be applied to other materials and structures that exhibit piezoresistive effects in engineering projects. 
The challenge of perfecting this method on actual projects remains the difficulty of conducting experimental tests that simulate real-world conditions while accurately detecting damage in self-sensing materials. 
However, the solution can be achieved by carrying out multiple tests with slight variations, thereby accountin for the variability of these materials. 
In the context of the developed algorithm, this issue is referred to as the variability of the forward problem. 
Multiple testing also enables the detection of damage configurations that the algorithm may miss, such as small holes, by carrying out post-mortem comparisons of test results and simulation data. 
This approach can be applied to other projects that utilize composite materials, from sports equipment to sailboats.

A theoretical model involving an intricate scalar field that connects to (electron, muon) or (muon, tau) pairs is considered within a certain "duration" window where the mass difference between two lepton types lies between their sum and the absolute difference. Although a moderately large interaction between this scalar field and the two lepton types could lead to extended lifetimes and larger observable distances between their birth and death points. By leveraging existing neutrino experiments and an upcoming one, we plan to explore various possible scenarios of this theoretical model. For instance, we can utilize data from the muonium decay rate and LSND production and decay patterns to evaluate this scalar's coupling, excluding the mass window indicated by the muon anomalous magnetic moment anomaly in the electron-muon sector. Furthermore, we analyze three major production processes of these scalar particles at beam dump experiments, such as the Drell-Yan process, heavy meson decay, and muon scattering, to derive constraints from the CHARM and NuTeV experiments and gauge the detection capabilities of the upcoming SHiP beam dump experiment which has the ability to exhaustively explore the mass window linked to the muon anomalous magnetic moment anomaly. In the electron-muon sector, we find that this scalar's lifetime must exceed 0.03 muon decay lengths or its mass must surpass 0.73 GeV, a value that approaches the mass of the tau lepton. On the other hand, in the muon-tau sector, we find that this scalar's lifetime must exceed 0.16 muon decay lengths or its mass must surpass 1.2 GeV, a value that surpasses the mass of the tau lepton. Both of these results hold true for interactions mediated by the neutral component of an electroweak doublet. In addition to this, we analyze the impact of this scalar on the muon anomalous magnetic moment, Lepton Universality, and the weak interaction, and also discuss possible ways to enhance the sensitivity of beam dump experiments to this theoretical model. We conclude by noting that this theoretical model could be related to the origin of the muon anomalous magnetic moment anomaly, incorporating Lepton Universality, and that future experiments such as the MESA, Muonium experiment at PSI, and the BES-III experiment will have the capability to either confirm or refute this model. We also provide three "duration" windows that define the conditions under which this scalar interacts with (electron, muon) or (muon, tau) pairs.

We demonstrate that Coxeter groups possess biautomatic properties, resulting from which we derive that uniform lattices within isometry groups of buildings also exhibit biautomatic structures. This conveys that these lattices have finitely many conjugacy classes of torsion elements. Moreover, this leads to the conclusion that they contain a subgroup isomorphic to a biautomatic group with finite index. Finally, by extending the concept of biautomaticity to graph groups, we show that a specific class of graph groups are biautomatic, resulting in the finite number of conjugacy classes of torsion elements within their lattices, and ultimately, a subgroup isomorphic to a biautomatic group with finite index. This in turn implies that these lattices have a specific 2-group structure, and enables us to precisely count the number of conjugacy classes of torsion elements within them. This further extends to the calculation of the number of conjugacy classes of a specific form within the lattice, allowing us to determine its rank. Lastly, this is demonstrated through explicit examples. The paper at large builds upon the preceding work of Bestvig, Davis, and Drutu, and the fundamental concept of biautomaticity on graph groups was initially discovered by Bestvig. The main contribution here involves generalising the conjugacy class calculation for a specific form of torsion elements within uniform lattices. The paper at large is organised as follows: chapter 2 provides an overview of the key terms and concepts employed throughout the paper; chapter 3 demonstrates that Coxeter groups are biautomatic; chapter 4 explores the implications of this for uniform lattices within isometry groups of buildings; chapter 5 examines the concept of graph groups and calculates the number of conjugacy classes of a specific form within uniform lattices; and chapter 6 applies this general concept to a range of lattice examples. The paper at large ends with an appendix containing supplementary material. The main contributors to the paper at large are Bestvig, whose work provided the foundation for the theory presented, and the first name author, who generalised the conjugacy class calculation for a specific form of torsion elements within uniform lattices. The second name author's role was minimal and consisted of providing a discussion on group theory and explaining the concept of biautomaticity. The paper at large was written in 2023. The paper at large is dedicated to the memory of the late professor, Marc Burger

Recent advances in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have made significant progress in recovering mobility in individuals with spinal cord injuries. Historically, these systems have focused on upper body function recovery but have given less attention to lower limb rehabilitation. Studies utilizing non-invasive electroencephalography (EEG) have explored the restoration of walking ability in paraplegia but have limitations in accurately decoding more complex aspects of gait due to EEG's restricted spatial and temporal resolution. To address this challenge, researchers utilized high-resolution electrocorticogram (ECoG) recordings from the motor cortices of healthy subjects while they walked on a treadmill. The analysis revealed a high level of accuracy (99.8%) in predicting walking state and step rate information from the recorded signals over extended periods (>16 minutes). Furthermore, incorporating a Bayesian filter method led to a high correlation between predicted and actual step rates (0.934), indicating a high potential for using this BCI in the safe control of modern prosthetic devices for walking. Overall, this study demonstrates the potential of this ECoG-based BCI in recovering autonomous walking in individuals with spinal cord injuries at different levels of mobility. Although limited to this instance, this study's results suggest similar BCIs could be developed for the recovery of other complex motor functions. The associated open-source software allows for easy replication and facilitates future studies on a broader range of subjects. The findings presented in this study have been featured in a previous conference report published by the author. The current work represents a comprehensive refined version of that initial report. In recent years, graph-based neural network methods, like graph neural networks, have effectively tackled classification and link prediction tasks by capturing complex data representations. However, most current applications rely on static graph models, which fail to account for the ever-changing connectivity structure observed in highly dynamic systems. Utilizing static models in such scenarios leads to subpar performance. In contrast, modeling temporal changes in graph structure offers a more comprehensive understanding, going beyond classification capabilities. Current approaches primarily focus on correlation-based representations, neglecting directed relationships, which are essential in numerous domains, particularly neuroscience. Our novel model, DECENNT, seeks to address this limitation by introducing a directed and dynamic graph, trained through neural network optimization, that reflects downstream classification and prediction tasks. DECENNT outperforms existing solutions in multiple tasks and provides task-specific dynamic graphs that are easily interpretable. When applied to neuroimaging data, DECENNT-generated graphs demonstrate high consistency with existing research and provide supplementary insights. Moreover, DECENNT's temporal attention mechanism identifies pivotal time periods for predictive downstream tasks from complex time series data. Lastly, our model's flexibility enables seamless integration into existing workflows, offering a suitable substitute for static models without requiring substantial workflow modifications. We publicly release DECENNT's code and an accompanying demonstration website to facilitate further research and incorporation into existing neuroimaging analyses. In a nutshell, DECENNT offers a versatile and high-performing solution for dynamic graph construction from multivariate time series data. We explore DECENNT's capabilities across multiple tasks, showcasing its potential applications in neuroscience, among other fields. Moreover, DECENNT's temporal attention-based design enables discovery of critical time periods essential for predicting downstream tasks from complex time series data. Finally, we present DECENNT-generated and manually examined dynamic graphs constructed from neuroimaging data, demonstrating the model's capability to accurately capture complex neural connections and distinguishing them into different categories, and comparing them with existing research on effective and ineffective connections. We also release DECENNT's code on GitHub at https://github.com/yash-sonar/DECENNT. For further information about DECENNT, please visit http://decennt.net/. For a video presentation of DECENNT, please see https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6s5sDGlwNpM. For a blog post introducing DECENNT, please see https://decennt.net/decennt-introduction/. Animals move through their environments for different purposes such as foraging, settling into a habitat, capturing prey, evading predators or mating. The vast array of biodiversity is linked to the diverse locomotory methods that different species employ, with many creatures using their legs, wings, fins, and other appendages to navigate their surroundings. This document refers to the movement of biological species as biolocomotion, presenting a computational method to automatically identify biolocomotion from raw video footage. A distinguishing feature of biolocomotion is its combination of forward movement and asymmetrical oscillatory motion, absent in the movement of non-living objects. By utilizing this trait along with differences between the overall movement of an object and the movement of its individual parts, a detection algorithm is created to determine whether the observed motion corresponds to a biological entity. Alternatively, a second approach based on a combination of common features and machine learning is presented for comparison purposes. A newly developed dataset consisting of a broad range of moving biological and non-biological objects in real-world settings, along with biolocomotion annotations for an existing dataset of camouflage animals, are provided to support the proposed detection method. Experimental results show that the proposed approach outperforms the alternative method, suggesting that biolocomotion can be accurately detected based on its distinctive movement patterns. This discovery has implications for fields such as biology, ecology, and conservation, where the ability to automatically identify moving biological species could be highly beneficial. A related video dataset along with implementation details are available online at https://github.com/abhishek79/biolocomotion_detection. System-administrators please note: MATLAB is required to run the code for biolocomotion detection. The proposed approach has been optimized to perform on a workstation with an i7 processor and 64 GB of RAM. The proposed algorithm takes approximately 30 hours to train on the animal dataset and approximately 5 seconds to detect biolocomotion in a single frame of the outdoor dataset. The advent of big data processing has created significant computational challenges when dealing with large-scale linear systems and matrix inversion, prompting the development of fast approximate iterative matrix inversion methods. Leveraging GPU acceleration, researchers have explored alternatives to classic direct inversion, leading to various methods such as Neumann Series, Newton iteration, and Successive Over-Relaxation. In response, we introduce a new iterative algorithm called 'Nested Neumann' (NN), which builds on the Neumann Series by incorporating a free iterative update of the preconditioning matrix, utilizing an inception depth to enhance convergence. Theoretical analysis has proven that NN meets three key conditions: it converges given the spectral norm condition is satisfied, achieves a convergence rate of one order higher for each additional inception depth, and has an optimal inception depth of one or two, subject to RAM constraints. Furthermore, we derive an explicit formula for the NN applicable to massive sparse matrices at an increased computational cost, demonstrating its analytic equivalence to higher-order iterations. The Nested Neumann method can be used for matrix inversion in positive semi-definite matrices and general linear systems, including sparse, non-sparse, and complex matrices. The paper also includes a discussion on optimizing parameters for the NN, along with a dataset-based recommendation. The accompanying code is publicly available on GitHub, allowing for easy implementation and customization of the Nested Neumann method. The paper concludes by analyzing the theoretical aspects and numerical results of the NN, indicating that the method compares favorably to other state-of-the-art methods, including GPU-accelerated sparse direct inversion, with achievable acceleration factors of twenty or more. The research has significant implications for a broad range of applications involving matrix inversion, including deep learning, simulated transponder navigation, and algorithmic trading. The Nested Neumann method has been found to be particularly effective for these contexts, where it can reduce computation time by fifty to ninety percent, along with achievable acceleration factors of twenty to thirty, following optimization of the method's parameters. The paper also discusses the relationship between the NN and other methods, including the Neumann Series, Newton iteration, and Successive Over-Relaxation, along with an analysis of the issues related to random initialization, batch processing, and the challenges of implementing the NN on complex sparse matrices, involving direct inversion of sparse matrices at the center of the NN. The research has identified several pathways for future development, including the development of a GPU-accelerated sparse matrix preconditioning library, the creation of a deep learning framework based on the NN, along with the integration of the NN

We examine topological and localization phenomena in one-dimensional systems with spatially correlated random disorders. This study explores the effect of binary disorders on a Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. Our findings show that binary disorders can induce a topological Anderson insulating phase in multiple parameter ranges. This insulating phase is distinguished by the disorder-averaged winding number and localized bulk states in real and momentum spaces. Our research demonstrates that the topological phase boundaries match those predicted by the self-consistent Born approach, while also analyzing the impact of correlated disorders on zero-energy mode localization and the topological Anderson phases. Additionally, we demonstrate that the topological characteristics can be identified by mean chiral displacement in atomic or photonic systems, providing an extension of previous work to include correlated disorders. Contextual linear bandits is an important model with various applications and has seen a significant surge in interest lately. This surge particularly occurred in the realm of wireless applications, where communication constraints pose a significant performance obstacle. Especially in scenarios where context dimensions are substantial. This paper addresses a decentralized, memoryless contextual linear bandit learning problem. In this problem, agents that observe the context and make decisions are physically isolated from the learner. This learner executes the learning process but remains unaware of the context. Contexts are assumed to be generated randomly and a new approach is presented. This approach uses approximately five context dimensions' worth of information when the context distribution is unknown and uses zero bits when the distribution is known. This approach offers nearly the same regret bound as if contexts were fully observable. This achievement is notable as it outperforms existing bounds by a significant margin. This achievement particularly occurred when the time horizon is substantial. When the distribution is known the approach offers an information theoretically optimal bound. This paper also presents a simple, decentralized context learning algorithm. This algorithm offers a worse but still manageable regret bound. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models of ground reaction forces through the resistive force theory (RFT). A feedforward force control system was developed and tested in conjunction with the DEM simulation. To account for discrepancies in the RFT model's predictions of ground reaction forces, a feedback control system was employed. As a result, the robot successfully tracked its intended trajectory, reached the desired height in five hops, and reduced height errors compared to a feedforward control system alone. Furthermore, by increasing the robot's foot area from 1cm^2 to 49cm^2, the feedback controller demonstrated its ability to adapt to changing ground reaction forces, even when the foot size was comparable to the diameter of individual grains. Additionally, this system's performance was tested under sudden ground changes and with different surface slopes. This research provides a method for efficiently simulating and optimizing complex ground reaction force interactions in a controlled environment. This is particularly relevant for applying optimization techniques to various aspects of the robot's performance. The code for this project is available online. In a broader context, this work offers a starting point for further investigation into the use of optimization techniques for enhancing performance in legged robots, as well as the development of improved force models for simulating real-world environments. extent to which it can be reduced to a simplified one-band Hubbard model. 
Screening of the $s$-like orbital's influence is a critical factor here. 
Without screening, an isolated highly-correlated band yields an
antiferromagnetic ground state. For mild screening, strong correlations cause
the more freely moving $s$-electrons to shift to the $d$-band and the nickelate
then becomes a half-filled, highly insulating state. This case is notably
distinct from high-$T_c$ cuprates, with $s$-wave symmetry being a more
expected phenomenon. 
On the other hand, strong screening leads to a mixture of filled and weakly
coupled $s$ and $d_{x^2-y^2}$ bands and results in self-doped $d$ orbital and
$d$-wave pairing tendencies emerging. 
Interestingly, strong screening allows for another one-band physics approximation,
this time incorporating significant weight transfer when an extra filled $s$-band
is included, exhibiting both one-band physics and Kondo-lattice-like behavior,
which arises solely from this single model. 
Ultimately, our comprehensive analysis highlights the intricate relationships
between weight transfer, screening, and the motion of electrons as well as the
robustness of possible $d$-wave pairing states within infinite layered nickelates.

electronic properties is also noted, along with the possibility of switching
between multiple states simultaneously, potentially through critical application
of dynamical strain. 
Therefore, infinite layered nickelates are found to possess an unique and
versatile physics that is sensitive to screening and motion of electrons, which
could be manipulated to reveal their conformable nature. 
A novel approach to describing this complex physics is proposed, involving a
combination of combined and separated $s$ and $d$ orbital bands, which may be
useful for understanding not just infinite layered nickelates but also other
related doped materials. 
Ultimately, our findings are expected to be applicable to other 4d and 5d
electron based materials.

This approach assesses hypothetical distortions in general relativity's influence on astronomical observations. A key factor influencing these measurements is a post-Newtonian parameter, denoted by $\gamma$, which measures the gravitational impact on light deflection. Analytical calculations of variable PPN $\gamma$'s effect on observables revealed that a change in this parameter causes a global shift in parallax measurements. This led us to develop a formula linking this shift to the satellite's position, the angle between its axis and the direction to the Sun, and the uncertainty of PPN $\gamma$. To effectively handle questions that require a broad range of background knowledge, it's common to incorporate external knowledge. However, utilizing limitless external knowledge often results in incorporating noisy and misleading information, posing a problem for machine-based answers. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel semantic-driven knowledge-aware question answering framework, designed to manage the injection of external knowledge with varying degrees of precision. Initially, the framework filters knowledge on the basis of a coarse understanding of the question's semantics, refining its search as necessary to ensure relevance and accuracy. The knowledge-aware approach is achieved through a combination of a semantic-aware knowledge retrieval module that incorporates structural information and prioritizes relevant knowledge. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through improved performance on the CommonsenseQA dataset, outperforming strong baselines in question answering accuracy. Moreover, the approach is extendable to other domain-specific knowledge-aware question answering tasks. The code for this approach is available at https://github.com/ghrua/CoarseToCareful.

Astronomical environments, particularly in comets, are rich in molecular cations whose exceptional brightness under UV to visible light can facilitate the understanding of local plasma environments and the composition of cometary neutral gas. Although molecular cations generally exhibit stronger and longer wavelength electronic emission than their neutral counterparts, comprehensive spectral models are hindered by existing limitations in data availability. For the most straightforward species, including oxygen-based molecules such as water, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, and hydroxyl, there are significant gaps in spectral reference data in some frequency ranges. As a result, cometary spectrum analysis remains incomplete and cannot fully account for the key processes involving these common comet molecules. This study gathers existing spectral information about these cations to pinpoint areas where additional research is necessary to enhance the comprehension of cometary evolution. It also highlights instances where certain cations are preferentially created over others, which can be inferred from spectral features in the UV to visible range, and presents a simple analytical model for predicting neutral gas compositions based on cation data, although further development is required for its refinement. Fill-in research on these molecules will significantly enrich our understanding of cometary evolution and can also contribute to similar studies concerning lunar regolith, asteroid samples, and planetary atmospheres. In the context of a Parameter Server, learning a model from distributed data on a graph is a challenging task, especially when it comes to Federated Learning. A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server. A common strategy used to address this issue involves each node making several local model updates before sharing the updated model with the server. Although this method reduces communication costs, it introduces statistical disparities among the nodes' data sets, leading to slower model convergence and biases. This paper explores the application of random walk learning algorithms to tackle these issues by exploiting existing connections between nodes, as they typically require less communication with the server. A random walk is proposed where a node shares the updated model with a neighbor, with the aim of visiting more informative nodes more frequently. This goal is framed as a sleeping multi-armed bandit problem to devise an efficient node sampling strategy that generates variance-reduced gradient estimates. A novel adaptive random walk learning algorithm is introduced and proven to converge theoretically. Moreover, our results demonstrate its superior performance compared to other random walk algorithms. The proposed method is further extended to heterogeneous data sets in multi-parameter settings, where the challenge lies in determining the number of parameters for each node. Knowledge tracing has seen significant advancements through deep learning-based models, however the underlying factors behind their success remain poorly understood. A primary challenge lies in comparing these approaches, due to the lack of standardization in data preprocessing procedures and evaluation protocols. These inconsistencies hinder real-world applicability in educational settings. To address these limitations, we present PyKT, a comprehensive Python-based platform for valid and standardized evaluations across various deep learning knowledge tracing methods. This benchmark platform incorporates a unified data preprocessing protocol across 7 diverse datasets and integrates 10 leading deep learning knowledge tracing model implementations, enabling transparent and reproducible experiments. Empirical studies conducted on PyKT highlight critical findings, including the risk of performance inflation caused by label leakage in certain evaluation settings, and the limited improvement achieved by several deep learning knowledge tracing models when compared to the initial approach proposed by Piech et al. We have publicly released PyKT and the associated research results at https://pykt.org/. We invite researchers and practitioners to collaborate with us and contribute to the advancement of deep learning knowledge tracing. We also provide a brief discussion on real-world practical considerations and theoretical limitations observable in the data.

Transfer learning has been proposed to overcome such challenges even across linguistic barriers, for example using a trained English model for German ASR. We explored this approach with much less related languages, specifically adapting an English model for Czech ASR, and discovered a simpler transfer method that significantly boosted the effectiveness. We used a modified alphabet without accents to make the transfer easier and observed this strategy to be extremely successful. Furthermore, our technique demonstrated potential when applied to Czech data alone, employing a coarse-to-fine training style. We were able to accomplish notable reductions in training time as well as the word error rate (WER). Our optimal model achieved a 14% reduction in WER without decrease in training time, a 5% reduction in WER with a 14% decrease in training time, and a 6% reduction in WER with a 24% decrease in training time. Our approach has been pre-trained models like BERT's counterparts, we suggest naming them BREAD (BERT's Recurrent Automatic Decoding Translation). Our code is available at https://github.com/martin-hannig/brad.

Most current sequence-to-sequence based Grammatical Error Correction methods focus primarily on generating more pseudo data to improve performance. In contrast, little work addresses the challenge of adapting GEC to new domains with limited resources. This paper treats various GEC domains as separate tasks and proposes a novel approach, grounded in meta-learning, that achieves few-shot domain adaptation without relying on pseudo data. Leveraging rich source domains, we establish a starting point for our model's parameters that facilitates efficient adaptation on scarce resource target domains. The proposed method is applied to adapting GEC models for the native languages of second language learners. To validate our approach, we utilized nine languages as source domains and five languages as target domains in the L1 GEC domain adaptation dataset, with results showing that it outperforms the baseline multi-task transfer learning approach by a 0.50 F score on average and enables successful adaptation to new target domains with as little as 200 parallel sentences. The code for this paper is available at https://github.com/ghrua/sentence-metadata-network.

The task of allocating non-divisible goods to self-interested agents, where the valuation functions add up, and without the possibility of making monetary transactions, presents an interesting problem in fair allocation. In our investigation, we focus on whether mechanisms exist that, regardless of the situation, produce equilibria that are fair allocations for the involved agents, using only their declared, rather than true values, as input. Specifically, we are examining whether mechanisms exist for two relaxations of envy-free allocation - namely, allocating one good (EF1) or any good (EFX) fairly. Through our exploration, we investigated two established methods for achieving these relaxed envy-free allocations in a non-selfish setting: Round-Robin, known for generating allocations that are fair up to one good for any number of agents, and a cut-and-choose method of Plaut and Roughgarden, known for generating allocations that are fair up to any good for two agents. In our investigation of Round-Robin, we discovered that all equilibria resulting from it are fair allocations that are up to one good with respect to their underlying values, whereas for the Plaut and Roughgarden method, we discovered that the corresponding allocations are fair up to any good, as well as satisfying a maximin share fairness condition. Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning often encounters issues due to differing levels of effectiveness among the agents' learned behavior. For example, if one agent has a random policy while the others are more skilled, existing offline methods can result in the team's performance suffering. To tackle this problem, we present a novel offline learning framework called Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) that explicitly considers the diversity of individual trajectories. The SIT framework leverages an attention-based mechanism and a graph attention network (GAT) to prioritize high-quality experiences and encourage sharing of effective trajectories among the agents. Through rigorous evaluation, our approach achieves superior results on complex datasets, especially in scenarios with significant variations in data quality. Our code is available at https://github.com/AI-Education/SIT.

We developed a novel approach for registering MV images, utilizing a Convolutional Neural Network, in both 2D and 3D. Traditional image registration techniques are largely intensity-based and leverage optimization algorithms to align images, yet they fall short for low-quality megavoltage images and have limited capture ranges. To overcome these challenges, we employed a Convolutional Neural Network, resulting in a dataset-based comparison using 50 brain images, which demonstrated improved results relative to conventional methods. Specifically, our evaluation showed a 23% decrease in DSC values compared to BHHC, a 21% decrease compared to ACWC, and a 26% decrease compared to LCCC in both 2D and 3D scenarios. Additionally, our network's capture range was significantly broader, with a 2D DSC value exceeding 0.75 for 87% of the brain images and 3D DSC value exceeding 0.75 for 85% of the brain images. We tested our network on 10 prostate images and found that 2D DSC values exceeded 0.75 for 90% of the brain images and 3D DSC values exceeded 75% for 80% of the brain images. We also explored a 2D-to-3D image registration approach and obtained a 2D DSC value exceeding 0.75 for 100% of the brain images and 3D DSC value exceeding 0.75 for 85% of the brain images. We validated our approach using public datasets and obtained comparable results. We hope this work serves as a foundation for incorporating spatial regularization and multi-resolution image registration in Convolutional Neural Networks. We have publicly released our code and a dataset of registered brain images at https://github.com/AmirPahanz/MVImageRegistration.

V392 Persei, classified as a dwarf nova that underwent a classic nova explosion in 2018, is an extraordinary object whose extreme evolution over nearly three years has been closely observed.  V392 Persei, which rapidly shrank from 2 days, exhibited early spectral characteristics pointing towards several massive ejections interacting and causing both gamma-ray and optical illumination through shock waves.  V392 Persei entered its Sun-constrained phase soon after its eruption but upon exiting it entered its nebular stage with evidence of the super-soft X-ray stage's lingering tail.  Post eruption spectra showed both a persistent narrow-line spectrum of the accretion disk as well as the fading of the ejected particles, which were illuminated by an intense ongoing X-ray emission.  Optical data reveal an orbital period of nearly three and a half days while the absence of the white dwarf spin frequency presents further evidence for a massive WD.  The pre and post nova energy distributions also indicate a massive accretion rate.  V392 Persei, unlike many novae and dwarf novae systems, did not switch to its initial low mass transfer configuration, but instead stayed in its high mass transfer state, which we believe is as a result of the irradiation of the companion by the massive nova explosion, thus it exhibits a level of similarity with another renowned system known as GK Persei.  The extensive observation of V392 Persei provides a thorough understanding of this system which could be achieved through the combination of semi analytical and hydro dynamic nova eruptions and dwarf nova instability models.  Additionally this extensive data set offers a suitable laboratory for studying both gamma-ray bright novae as well as the long duration sun constrained phase.  V392 Persei which is located in the gamma-ray line detector field of view provides the largest sample of gamma-ray bright novae known to date, with a gamma-ray brightness that is nearly an order of magnitude greater than any other nova recorded by this detector.  The extensive observation of V392 Persei also provides a particular opportunity for the direct observation of the gamma-ray bright phase's termination, which could offer further understanding on this phase as well as on the long duration sun constrained phase that follows it.  The analysis of this system's energy distribution as well as orbital period presents further evidence for a massive accretion rate, which could be achieved through the combination of semi analytical and hydro dynamic dwarf nova and nova eruptions instability and interaction models.  The extensive observation of V392 Persei could also be described as a particular long duration sun constrained phase nova

Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then creates a codebook based on GMM components, assigning one entry per component. Only the GMM is transferred to the mobile terminal, allowing it to find the most relevant codebook entry by measuring the responsibility of each GMM component to the received signal, without needing channel estimation. Our framework accounts for the movement of Population III binary remnants during the formation of the universe's structure and identifies which of these remnants fall into nuclear star clusters through gravitational interaction with field stars. Following this, we track their subsequent development within these clusters through gravitational encounters and gravitational waves, and predict the likelihood of mergers of Population III binary remnants. Our study shows that about 7.5% of Population III binary remnants become situated in the centres of galaxies and 5-50% of these will merge in nuclear star clusters at high redshifts. These events peak at z=5-7 with a merger rate of 0.4-10 years^-1 Gpc^-3. Our predictions also reveal that the most massive of these remnants primarily reside in small, low-mass nuclear star clusters formed in the early universe. These clusters host black holes of masses 40-85 M_\\odot that can produce detections similar to GW190521, specifically in a mass range typically found for pulsational pair-instability supernovae with a merger rate of 0.01-0.09 years^-1 Gpc^-3. The expected signals from these events will provide valuable insights into the early universe and its structure. One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.

Deep learning models such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have been highly effective in various sequence analysis tasks but suffer from limitations in their practical application due to their size. This problem is particularly pronounced in video recognition, which involves high-dimensional data. In an attempt to overcome these constraints and unlock the full potential of LSTMs, this research proposes an integrated design of algorithms and hardware to achieve high-performance, energy-efficient LSTM networks. At the algorithmic level, a new LSTM structure called FDHT-LSTM is developed, which significantly reduces model complexity without sacrificing accuracy. In addition to this optimized algorithm, a customized hardware platform is also designed to efficiently execute the FDHT-LSTM model by incorporating a sophisticated memory access scheme that minimizes data conflicts and allows for real-time matrix transformations. Experimental results indicate that the compact FDHT-LSTM models and the hardware accelerator exhibit high performance, outperforming existing compressed LSTM models by an order of magnitude in terms of model size while also demonstrating substantial improvements in accuracy across multiple video recognition datasets. Furthermore, the proposed FDHT-LSTM architecture is found to excel over a leading tensor decomposed hardware model called TIE in terms of throughput, area efficiency, and energy efficiency in various benchmark tests. The energy-efficient FDHT-LSTM network has been fabricated into a Field-Programmable Gate Array (FPGA) chip, which is capable of real-time video recognition processing. The open-source FDHT-LSTM algorithm is compatible with multiple deep learning frameworks such as Caffe, TensorFlow, and PyTorch, allowing seamless model porting and easy integration into various customized hardware platforms. The proposed FDHT-LSTM network has vast applications in various high-speed, real-time video analysis tasks that require energy and area efficiency. The compact FDHT-LSTM models, combined with the hardware accelerator, demonstrate the benefits of integrated design of algorithms and hardware in other contexts that involve similar trade-off challenges. The concept of the Weak Gravity Conjecture is often expressed through its effect on the mass-to-charge ratio of a particle. Another approach posits its fundamental expression is tied to the self-repulsive properties of a specific particle in long-range interactions. A new, closely related formulation suggests it could be formulated in terms of a particle's self-binding energy, which must remain non-negative. This new interpretation becomes particularly insightful within anti-de Sitter space due to its association with a conformal field theory, where a relationship involving the dimension of an operator exists and forms a convex function of the operator's charge under a U(1) symmetry. The rapid transformation of the electricity sector necessitates innovative ancillary services that guarantee the stability and dependability of the electricity network. Unfortunately, evaluations and policy advice concerning ancillary services and market structures lack methods for examining the intricate interplay between markets and services. Consequently, this study presents an open-source agent-based model to evaluate design options for ancillary services and electricity markets. The Ancillary Services Acquisition Model integrates the MESA agent-based modeling framework with the PyPSA Python toolset for Power System Analysis. This model offers adjustable market parameters, agent-specific tactics, and thorough clearing algorithms for the day-ahead market, continuous intra-day trading, redispatch, and imbalance management. Furthermore, the model includes multiple policy performance indicators, including a novel pricing multiplier and new redispatch performance indicators. The results from a stylized simulation scenario validated the model and explored a redispatch design issue, revealing several key implications. The findings indicate that, when implementing order types in multi-period redispatch markets, the following effects are produced: the risk is minimized for market participants due to complete order fulfillment, but this may lead to increased trading of imbalances during intra-day and dispatch ramp risks, resulting from large orders; meanwhile, the grid operator over-procures redispatch during peak periods when all-or-none design is employed, which can also lead to induced imbalances due to inadequate redispatch activation. The model and results also highlight the significance of examining intra-day dynamics and the potential side effects of redispatch and imbalance management on markets, as well as the necessity for robust methodological tools to evaluate and design ancillary services and electricity markets. The model is available online at https://github.com/ancillaryservices/acquisition_model.

R.W.K. Odoni initially established the connection between the Galois group of an iterated polynomial and the symmetric group in fields of characteristic zero. A generalization to fields of positive characteristic was achieved by Juul. Building on these findings, we explore a scenario involving an irreducible polynomial F over the algebraic closure of a finite field k(t) with algebraic and separable coefficients. When a generic monic polynomial Phi is composed with F, resulting in a new polynomial with coefficients (a0, a1,...), we identify the Galois group of the composite polynomial's mth iterate. The structure of this Galois group mirrors the (m-folded) iterated wreath product of the symmetric group S_(nd) for n > 0, where n represents the polynomial's degree. In the case of large finite fields, the application of this discovery aligns with analogous theories, including the polynomial equivalent of the Bateman-Horn conjecture, the Chowla's conjecture regarding autocorrelation, and the Chebotarev density theorem over function fields. The investigation also involves a specific polynomial F_3 of degree three, leading to some notable outcomes, including an infinite set of prime values n such that the mth iterate of F_3 is reducable for prime numbers n dividing (t\^n - 1)/(t-1). Furthermore, a connection is established between the prime factorization of the composite polynomial's mth iterate and the properties of a specific set of polynomials, thereby providing a proof of the implied infinity of prime specialization values n. The study finally concludes with some open problems, including a general form for the prime factorization of the composite polynomial's mth iterate, the determination of the mth iterate's reduction type for an infinite set of prime values n, the verification of the proposed infinity of prime specialization values n, and the extension of the findings to general polynomial scenarios. The paper at large highlights an novel approach combining number theory and algebraic geometry, yielding an interesting biological application. The strongest of these appear during Saturn's summer and disappear in the winter. The extensive exploration of the Saturn system enabled by the Cassini spacecraft has facilitated a comprehensive study of the formation of the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex through the application of infrared spectroscopy. By analyzing this phenomenon, researchers were able to identify the rates of formation and dissolution of these polar vortices in both hemispheres. The vortex in the north began forming in the late spring, but it took until the end of the summer for it to exhibit the temperature and chemical contrasts seen in the southern hemisphere during its own summer. The vortex in the north was found to be surrounded by a strengthening temperature gradient at 78 degrees latitude and displayed a hexagonal shape. This indicates that a particular type of atmospheric wave, previously thought to influence temperatures deep in the planet's atmosphere, has the ability to impact temperatures as high as 300 km above the clouds. The dissolution of these vortices usually occurs in the fall, but the extent of this phenomenon is yet to be studied. We introduce a novel mixed finite element approach for single-phase Darcy flow within a fractured porous media, incorporating two types of fractures. These fractures can be viewed as interfaces within a $d$-dimensional space, where $d$ equals either $2$ or $3$. A significant distinction is drawn between fractures with notably high and low permeability compared to their surrounding medium, categorized as conductive and blocking fractures respectively. Our proposed method uses traditional hybrid-dimensional techniques to model conductive fractures and a more recent Dirac-$\delta$ function approach for blocking fractures. This results in our numerical scheme being compatible with nonconforming meshes in regards to the blocking fractures. A major advancement of our approach, the method also achieves conservative and symmetric results with regards to pressure. This methodology's effectiveness is demonstrated through the execution of numerous test cases across both two and three-dimensional settings. Our numerical data indicates that our approach offers highly comparable performance to existing literature methods. The proposed method's strengths are further highlighted by its ability to accurately represent blocking fractures without the need for thin traction layers. The underlying numerical principles and the presented examples' mathematical formulations are also outlined in the paper. The code used for the simulations has been made publicly available. The proposed method offers potential applications in solving a wide range of geophysical problems involving complex fracture networks. Hypothesis evaluation plays a significant role in cognitive science, where Bayes factors can compare and contrast competing theories by assessing their consistency with available data. However, implementing Bayes factor analysis is often complicated and heavily dependent on the accuracy of computational methods, as well as assumptions related to the model and data. We aim to investigate these challenges in cognitive science using Bayes factor analysis, focusing on the underlying statistical concepts and the need for objective utility functions to make informed decisions. We explore various issues with Bayes factor estimates, including their tendency to err and the reliability of bridge sampling, especially when analyzing complex scenarios. To tackle these challenges, we develop a simulation-based approach for validating the accuracy of Bayes factor estimates and examine the stability of Bayes factors in relation to different Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) draws. We also investigate the variability of Bayes factor estimates and the effectiveness of utility functions in making informed decisions. To facilitate the assessment of Bayes factor reliability, we outline a step-by-step workflow that researchers can use to evaluate the performance of Bayes factor analysis for their individual studies, including an illustrative example from the cognitive sciences. We anticipate that this research will contribute to the development of a robust methodology for evaluating scientific hypotheses based on Bayes factor analysis, along with reproducible code available online. This study provides a framework for evaluating the performance of Bayes factor analysis that can be applied across a broad range of fields, where Bayes factor analysis is used as an investigative tool. Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the identification of connections between sentences. To improve the effectiveness of sentence representations in classification tasks, research has been done on predicting these indicators between sentences. This work diverges from this approach by using a trained model to forecast suitable indicators between sentences that have an established semantic connection, based on existing datasets used for classification tasks. These predictions enable researchers to investigate the relationship between discourse indicators and the annotated semantic relations. Existing studies have established correlations between indicators and discourse relationships but are limited to specific instances and categories. On the other hand, numerous discourse indicators convey diverse relations and a universally accepted classification system does not exist. To rectify this, an automatic prediction method is applied to pre-existing semantically annotated datasets, leading to a novel characterization of discourse indicators in the English language, and a resulting dataset named DiscSense which is available for public use. Experimental evaluations have validated the accuracy of DiscSense, and the findings are expected to contribute to the development of rigorous standards for the classification of English discourse indicators. Furthermore, DiscSense is available at https://github.com/THUQH/DiscSense.

We investigate a general matrix optimization problem subject to a fixed-rank positive semidefinite constraint and perform the Burer-Monteiro factorization to analyze its landscape under a particular Riemannian quotient geometry. Assuming standard strong convexity and smoothness properties for the objective function f, we find that its factorized version exhibits distinct behaviors in three regions: (1) near the target parameter of interest, it is geodesically strongly convex and smooth; (2) it has neighborhoods of strict saddle points; and (3) it has large gradients in remaining areas. We contribute a global landscape analysis under the Riemannian quotient geometry for the first time and provide a geometric explanation for the effectiveness of vanilla gradient descent in this setting. When f satisfies a weaker convexity property, we discover a geodesically convex neighborhood around local minimizers. To achieve these results, we analyze a matrix factorization problem with a least squares objective, providing a critical connection, and also establish an independent result regarding the convexity of geodesic balls under the Riemannian quotient geometry. Finally, our work's implications are demonstrated on a matrix factorization problem with a least squares objective and the negative log-likelihood function of the Gaussian mixture model. The proposed work combines elements from optimization, geometry, and machine learning to address the matrix factorization problem's landscape under a particular Riemannian quotient geometry. Introducing "social-learning" variations of two algorithms led to successful attainment of Nash Equilibrium, unlike "individual learning" counterparts which consistently failed to converge to the desired outcome. Utilizing simulation outcomes with a specific approach as well as general statistical analysis, our results showed that "social" learning versions resulted in an ergodic Markov Chain, characterized by frequent occurrence of states leading to NE play in the stationary distribution. In contrast, "individual learning" failed to reach the NE state in our simulations, exhibited significantly greater distance from the desired NE state, required substantially longer time to reach the NE state, and displayed reduced robustness. Ultimately, our findings confirmed that the majority of games reached a Nash Equilibrium when players used the "social" learning algorithms. We also assessed the impact of different parameters on the algorithms and discussed our key cultural findings. Our research contributed to the limited existing literature on genetic algorithm-based Cournot models. Furthermore, our findings have implications for other contexts beyond economics, such as psychology and sociology, where similar co-evolutionary processes occur. Lastly, our work provided a prototype of a "teacher" algorithm that could be utilized to enhance learning in a wide range of contexts, not limited to economics. We also offered a mathematical approach for assessing convergence in simple forms, as well as a novel way of analyzing simulation outcomes in the statistics section. Ultimately, our research highlighted the positive outcomes achievable when players engage in mutual learning, consistent with the intuitive prediction of the desired economic outcome. Consider a weighted directed graph, denoted as $\mathcal{D}$, and the edge ideal associated with it, labeled as $I(\mathcal{D})$. We establish in this study that the symbolic and ordinary power series of $I(\mathcal{D})$ share the same equivalence for a specific subclass of weighted directed trees. Moreover, the paper also identifies both the required and sufficient conditions under which the symbolic and ordinary power series of oriented line segments exhibit equal behavior. Specifically for oriented line segments, we find that this equal behavior occurs in the $n$th symbolic and the $n$th ordinary power series for $n=2$ and $n=3$, whereas it holds true for all natural numbers $n$ if the directed path contains at least one loop. Additionally, a key polynomial factorization is obtained from the comparison of the symbolic and ordinary power series of weighted directed trees. We build a unified vocabulary space that spans multiple languages using the concept of distributional semantics. This approach enables seamless knowledge sharing and resource transfer between languages, extending beyond the realm of word-to-word translations. Our innovation includes aligning word clusters across languages and ensuring that the structure of these clusters remains consistent across different languages. We extract three key factors that influence clustering: neighboring words within each language's word space, character-level attributes, and linguistic patterns, which can be leveraged from knowledge bases available for over a thousand languages. We employ a novel cluster-consistent neural network to construct this unified vocabulary space by synchronizing words and their clusters. Our results show substantial gains in intrinsic evaluations of monolingual and multilingual semantic tasks, surpassing the performance of current multilingual embedding techniques. Moreover, an extrinsic evaluation using a case study on low-resource language name tagging demonstrates a remarkable 24.5% improvement in F-score compared to the existing state-of-the-art methods. Our pre-trained models and data are available at: \url{https://github.com/ghrua/MCSECSE}.

In late October 2019, violent disturbances and extensive infrastructure damage ravaged Chile's capital, particularly in Santiago. This project aims to adapt an epidemiological model previously applied to 2005's French riots to incorporate Santiago's subway layout and accurately depict the reported geographic spread of riots within the city. The existing model simulated the disorders' temporal progression with reasonable accuracy but struggled to replicate the observed distribution of unrest in Santiago. A key limitation hindering this model's effectiveness in capturing the city's rioting patterns appears to be the absence of a mechanism representing population displacement. This limitation is also reflected in the model's results, which show that the distribution of riots is predominantly centered on the subway system's busiest hubs, yet this aspect does not account for the extreme level of concentration observed in Santiago. A notable alignment is observed between the model's ability to replicate riots' temporal progression and the accuracy of its predictions, with an R-squared value of 0.86+0.05 for both the model and the prediction, respectively. A recent adaptation of the model incorporating an explicit migration parameter does indeed capture the distribution of unrest in Santiago, as evidenced by the model's simulated distribution and the actual rioting patterns reported in the media, with a relative Gini coefficient of 0.53+0.05. Notably, this model also predicts that increasing migration transmission rates above a certain threshold will shift the distribution of riots towards a more homogeneous pattern, as indicated by a low Alshculer index of 0.23+0.03. A further analysis of the model's results reveals that the decline in riots in Santiago occurred approximately two weeks after the disturbances' initial outbreak, a finding that is also reflected in the time it took for a similar decline to occur in Paris during the 2005 riots. A key difference between the two settings, however, lies in the distribution of unrest in Paris, which persisted even after the disturbances had subsided. This persistence is attributed to a higher transmission rate among population subgroups in Paris, which is also reflected in the model's results, with a more pronounced concentration of riots in the city's central areas even after the initial decline. This research develops an innovative method for addressing the containment issue with enhanced regular expressions, expanding basic patterns by integrating intersection and complement operators and incorporating regular expressions over infinitely vast character sets. Unlike traditional methods for containment assessment, this algorithm acknowledges the extended features and character sets in its calculations, bypassing the necessity to translate to automata equivalents and utilizing instead a symbolic rewriting system to solve inequality problems with regular expressions. We introduce a new approach to determining containment using a combination of Brzozowski's regular expression derivatives and Antimirov's rewriting strategy, along with an expansion of Brzozowski's derivative operator that accommodates (potentially infinite) sets of recognizable characters. We also explore the application of our method to regular expressions over finite character sets, revealing that it yields a decidable problem. Moreover, we investigate the containment problem using a theoretical framework that facilitates complexity analysis but requires a more abstract representation, showing that it is equivalent to the problem of determining whether a string lies within a language defined by a regular language equipped with an integer-modulo operator, and demonstrating that this results in a co-NP class of problems. We have implemented our method in a proof-of-concept solver called DeepRE, and have further research plans to enhance DeepRE and explore its potential uses in fields like formal verification and networking, in addition to its current role in educating theory students. We have also developed a series of educational materials to accompany the solver, designed for undergraduate students studying the theory of regular languages. Alongside this, we have presented an unpublished result that the problem of determining containment for regular languages defined by finite automata with reset actions is decidable, and have outlined a more complex approach that involves the use of game theory to determine containment for regular languages defined by finite automata with integer-modulo operations. This research has been published in the proceedings of the 27th International Conference on Fun with Algorithms, and the associated technical report is available with the ACM Digital Library. The solver DeepRE, along with the educational materials and the related technical report, are available online. The research has also been presented at the annual conference of the Australian Computing Society. The associated technical report is available with the arXiv repository. Mobile agents require accurate and robust localization, and to meet this demand, Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) algorithms have been developed to estimate positions and movements using both camera and inertial sensors' data. These models, in particular the deep learning-based VIO ones, offer the potential to provide pose information without the need to craft custom algorithms. Presently, the majority of VIO models using learning techniques, often rely on recurrent models that fuse multimodal information and process signals, although they have difficulty training and efficiency limitations. This paper proposes an external memory attention learning-based VIO framework, capable of efficiently combining the data from both the camera and inertial sensors for state estimation, and we demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of this model by accurately estimating the pose in various challenging scenarios, surpassing even the traditional and current state-of-the-art VIO baselines in various scenes. The proposed method's superiority is also proven by showing that it can handle difficult situations like wide motion basins and dense forests. The code is available at https://github.com/zhengyangyin/EMA-VIO.

Quantum mechanics relies on linear algebra, but nonlinear operators can lead to groundbreaking findings under specific conditions. In this study, we develop a new theoretical framework based on the parent Hamiltonians of the Weyl semimetal, which we call square-root higher-order Weyl semimetal, or SHOWS for short. SHOWS is characterized by both "Fermi-arc" surfaces and hinge states connecting Weyl point projections. By constructing a 3D solid-state model with honeycomb-kagome structures and double-helix layer couplings, we both theoretically and experimentally verify the exotic SHOWS state, thereby paving the way for realizing the square-root topological properties in 3D solid-state systems. Both theoretical and experimental findings can be generalized to higher-order semimetals, suggesting that honeycomb-kagome structures and double-helix layer couplings may lead to the discovery of other square-root topological states. Finally, we outline potential modifications to tailor SHOWS into a topological insulator or an ideal Weyl semimetal. This paper introduces the Federated Selective Aggregation (FedSA) challenge, a novel approach that allows the creation of a student model for a specific task by incorporating information from multiple unconnected teachers who have trained on various projects. Our focus on FedSA originates from the common obstacle encountered when attempting to exchange model data. Researchers and organizations typically invest significant resources in developing powerful neural networks but, due to data protection, cybersecurity concerns, or ownership restrictions, they cannot freely share their trained models, despite wishing to contribute to the community. To address this challenge, we propose the FedSA approach, taking it one step further as it enables a student to excel in a different task than the teachers from which it draws information. To effectively handle FedSA, we implemented a custom technique where the student model is created using a saliency-based method that allows it to selectively engage with relevant teachers and incorporate their unique features. To validate the FedSA model, we conducted comprehensive experiments under both single-task and multi-task settings, and our findings show that FedSA successfully combines knowledge from disparate sources, outperforming comparable centralized models. The resulting code is now available online, awaiting the contribution of model owners who can help further develop the FedSA framework. Moreover, we outline possible solutions for converting existing teacher models into ones suitable for FedSA. Lastly, we discuss the implications of FedSA for the artificial neural network community and beyond. All code is available at https://github.com/Abdullah-1/FedSA.

We investigate the minimal time it takes for a qubit state to evolve from an initial state into a distinguishable state under both unitary and non-unitary dynamics. For unitary dynamics generated by a time-independent Hamiltonian, we develop a crucial criterion involving two asymmetry measures that ensures a state can be distinguished from its unitary evolution with a specific error probability within a certain time. This condition enables us to rank qubit states by their distinguishability time and calculate the optimal time to release a two-level system as seen in the Landau-Zener problem. For non-unitary dynamics, we compare several bounds on distinguishability time, including a novel lower bound related to the system-environment asymmetry and expressed in terms of a specific matrix norm. This study also explores connections to the eigenvalue gap, system-environment entanglement, and the accuracy of the Hamiltonian. Additionally, we discuss several explicit examples of qubit states to illustrate these concepts. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between the eigenvalue gap and distinguishability time, demonstrating that the latter can vary smoothly with time, even when the eigenvalue gap vanishes, as well as exploring under which conditions the eigenvalue gap remains a reliable indicator of distinguishability time. Lastly, we determine the optimal time to release a system in a Landau-Zener problem, as well as in a situation with continuous driving, and show that the eigenvalue gap provides a steady-state estimate of distinguishability time in a thermal state. This work further examines the thermal state, for which the asymptotic time is found to be directly proportional to the temperature, with the proportionality constant related to the specific matrix norm and system properties.
